title: A1C goals bend to avoid lows
advice: The usual A1C goal is about 7% or a bit under. Guidelines are clear that it should be relaxed when lows are frequent or severe. A slightly higher A1C with far fewer lows is a better result.
how: ADA: A1C below 7% for many adults without significant hypoglycemia, and less stringent goals (for example below 8%) for those with frequent or severe lows or unawareness. Diabetes Canada: 7.0% or below for most; 7.1-8.5% for people with recurrent severe hypoglycemia or unawareness. Time in range and time below range on CGM now sit alongside A1C.
why: A1C is an average, so it can look good while lows cancel out highs, which hides danger.
sources: ADA Standards of Care 2026, Sec. 6, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc26-S006
Diabetes Canada CPG Ch. 8 Targets for Glycemic Control, 2018, https://www.diabetes.ca/for-professionals/full-guidelines/chapter-8

title: After the low: the follow-up snack
advice: Once you're back above 4, eat your usual meal if it's due. If the next meal is more than an hour away, have a small snack with some carbs and protein so you don't slide down again.
how: Diabetes Canada Rec. 8: once the low is reversed, eat the usual meal or snack due at that time. If the meal is more than 1 hour away, have a snack with 15 g of carbohydrate plus protein (for example 7 crackers with cheese, or 1 slice of bread with peanut butter). This matters most overnight and when a lot of insulin is still active.
why: The fast sugar is used up within about an hour, while long-acting and recent rapid insulin keep working.
sources: Diabetes Canada CPG Ch. 14 Hypoglycemia, Rec. 8, 2018, https://www.diabetes.ca/for-professionals/full-guidelines/chapter-14

title: How clinicians read an AGP report
advice: When an endocrinologist opens your report, they check that there's enough data, then go straight to the lows: when they happen and how deep they go. Only after that do they look at highs and then at the swings.
how: Step 1: confirm 14 days of data with 70% or more sensor wear. Step 2: time below range, and which time blocks it falls in (overnight, late morning, after meals). Step 3: time above range and the time of day of the highs. Step 4: variability (CV; the width of the shaded 25-75% and 5-95% bands). Step 5: tie each pattern to insulin timing, food and activity. Fix one pattern at a time, starting with the lows.
why: Highs are often caused by lows (rebound and over-treatment) and by fear of going low, so fixing the lows first takes away the reason for many of the highs.
sources: Danne T et al., International Consensus on Use of Continuous Glucose Monitoring, Diabetes Care 2017, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc17-1600
Battelino T et al., International Consensus on Time in Range, Diabetes Care 2019, https://doi.org/10.2337/dci19-0028

title: Ask about an automated insulin system
advice: Given how many lows you're having, it's worth asking your team about an automated insulin delivery (AID) system: a pump that talks to your Dexcom and turns insulin down when you're heading low. Guidelines now recommend offering these to adults with type 1.
how: ADA 2026: offer automated insulin delivery to all adults with T1D who can use it safely. Systems available in Canada work with Dexcom (for example Omnipod 5, t:slim X2 Control-IQ). Provincial pump programs (for example Ontario ADP) cover much of the cost; ask your clinic how to be referred. Overnight is where these systems help most.
why: Automated systems adjust basal insulin every 5 minutes based on CGM readings and can suspend it before a low.
sources: ADA Standards of Care 2026, Sec. 7 Diabetes Technology, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc26-S007
Holt RIG et al., ADA/EASD T1D Consensus, Diabetes Care 2021, https://doi.org/10.2337/dci21-0043

title: Alcohol and delayed lows
advice: Alcohol can cause a low many hours later, often overnight or the next morning, even if you went to bed with a good number. Drink with food, have a snack before bed, and set your alerts higher.
how: Eat carbs while drinking and don't drink on an empty stomach. Be careful with corrections for highs from sugary drinks. Go to bed above about 7 mmol/L with a carb-plus-protein snack. Raise the Dexcom low alert for that night. Tell someone with you that you have T1D, because a low can look like being drunk. Glucagon works less well after more than 2 drinks. The risk window lasts up to about 24 hours.
why: While the liver is busy clearing alcohol, it stops making new glucose, which removes the body's main defence against an overnight low.
sources: ADA Standards of Care 2026, Sec. 5 Facilitating Positive Health Behaviors, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc26-S005
Diabetes Canada CPG Ch. 14 Hypoglycemia, 2018, https://www.diabetes.ca/for-professionals/full-guidelines/chapter-14
Diabetes Canada CPG Ch. 11 Nutrition Therapy, 2018, https://www.diabetes.ca/for-professionals/full-guidelines/chapter-11

title: Eat while you drink
advice: Having food with alcohol is one of the simplest ways to make drinking safer with T1D. It also helps you notice and treat lows, since alcohol symptoms and low symptoms can look alike.
how: Plan to drink with a meal or snack containing carbs. Avoid drinking on an empty stomach or after exercise. If you've had more than a couple of drinks, check before bed and consider a snack with 15-30 g of slow carbs plus protein.
why: Food provides absorbed glucose while the liver's own glucose output is suppressed by alcohol.
sources: Diabetes Canada. Alcohol and diabetes, n.d., https://diabetes.ca/managing-my-diabetes/tools---resources/alcohol

Tetzschner R et al. Effects of alcohol on plasma glucose and prevention of alcohol-induced hypoglycemia in type 1 diabetes: systematic review with GRADE. Diabetes Metab Res Rev, 2018, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=Tetzschner+alcohol+hypoglycemia+type+1+GRADE

title: Plan for a low after drinking, even hours later
advice: A glass or two of wine with dinner can drop you in the night or next morning, because your liver gets busy clearing alcohol instead of releasing sugar.
how: Eat carbs with drinks, have a slower snack (toast with peanut butter, crackers and cheese) before bed even if you're in range, set the overnight Low alert a bit higher, and ask your husband to keep an eye on Follow. Some people discuss reducing basal or dinner insulin on drinking nights with their team.
why: Alcohol suppresses the liver's glucose output for up to 12-24 hours.
caveat: Beer and sweet drinks may raise you first, then drop you later. Glucagon is less effective after heavy drinking.
sources: Joslin Diabetes Center, 'Drinking with type 1: four tips', 2020, https://joslin.org/news-stories/all-news-stories/education/2020/12/drinking-type-1-four-tips-making-it
JDRF/Breakthrough T1D, 'Alcohol and Type 1 Diabetes: How to Manage a Night Out and the Morning After', https://www.jdrf.org/?p=138291
Diabetes UK Forum, 'Red wine' thread, https://forum.diabetes.org.uk/boards/threads/red-wine.78531

title: Beer vs wine vs spirits
advice: Different drinks act differently: regular beer, cider and coolers carry carbs that can raise glucose at first, while dry wine and straight spirits have little carb and lean toward lows later.
how: Approximate carbs: regular beer (341 mL) 10-15 g, light beer 3-6 g, dry wine (150 mL) 3-5 g, spirits 0 g, coolers/cider 20-35 g, mixed with regular pop 25-40 g. Many people choose not to fully dose for drink carbs because of the later-low risk - talk with your team about your approach.
why: Carbs in drinks raise glucose early, while the alcohol itself lowers it hours later, so the net effect depends on the drink.
sources: Diabetes Canada. Alcohol and diabetes, n.d., https://diabetes.ca/managing-my-diabetes/tools---resources/alcohol

Tetzschner R et al. Effects of alcohol on plasma glucose and prevention of alcohol-induced hypoglycemia in type 1 diabetes: systematic review with GRADE. Diabetes Metab Res Rev, 2018, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=Tetzschner+alcohol+hypoglycemia+type+1+GRADE

title: Sugar-free sweeteners
advice: Health Canada-approved sweeteners like sucralose, aspartame and stevia don't raise blood sugar and are a reasonable way to keep a sweet coffee without the carbs. Guidelines see them as fine in moderation, especially to replace sugar.
how: Use sweetener in coffee instead of sugar to save ~4 g carbs per teaspoon. Watch 'sugar alcohols' (maltitol, sorbitol) in sugar-free candy - they can still raise glucose a bit and cause tummy upset. Keep regular pop for treating lows, diet pop for everyday.
why: Non-nutritive sweeteners are not metabolized into glucose, so they have negligible glycemic effect.
sources: Diabetes Canada CPG Ch.11 Nutrition Therapy (Sievenpiper et al.), 2018, https://guidelines.diabetes.ca/cpg/chapter11
Evert AB et al. Nutrition Therapy for Adults With Diabetes or Prediabetes: A Consensus Report. Diabetes Care, 2019, https://doi.org/10.2337/dci19-0014
WHO. Use of non-sugar sweeteners guideline, 2023, https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240073616

title: Go easy on corrections at bedtime
advice: A big correction right before bed is a common hidden cause of a 3 a.m. low. If you're high at bedtime, a more cautious correction is usually safer. Ask your team how they'd like you to handle bedtime highs.
how: Check when you last took rapid insulin; if it was within about 3-4 hours, some of it is still working. Ask your team for a 'bedtime correction rule' (many use a reduced correction or a higher threshold at night). If you do correct, set the Dexcom low alert higher that night. The exercise consensus specifically advises against a correction near bedtime after exercise.
why: Insulin taken at bedtime peaks while you're asleep and not noticing symptoms, often on top of insulin still active from supper.
sources: Moser O et al., Glucose management for exercise using CGM and isCGM in T1D: EASD/ISPAD position statement, Diabetologia 2020, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00125-020-05263-9

title: Skip chocolate, cookies and peanut butter as low treatments
advice: It's tempting to grab whatever's around, but fat slows sugar down, so you stay low longer and then eat more.
how: Save chocolate and cookies for after you're back over 4.0. Treat with something fat-free first (tabs, juice, candies), then if a meal is far off, have a small protein snack.
why: Fat delays stomach emptying, so the carbs arrive late, often after you've already over-treated.
sources: DiabetesNet (Walsh), 'Low blood sugar treatment', https://www.diabetesnet.com/diabetes-control/low-blood-sugars/treatment/
diaTribe, 'Defeating the Hypoglycemia Binge', https://diatribe.org/diabetes-management/defeating-hypoglycemia-binge

title: Fewer lows can bring back your warning signs
advice: If you've noticed you don't feel lows the way you used to, there's real hope: a few weeks of carefully avoiding lows often brings some of those warning symptoms back.
how: People aim to keep everything above ~4.0-4.5 for 2-4 weeks (slightly higher targets, earlier alerts, careful corrections) and many report shakes and sweats returning.
why: Each low resets the brain's threshold lower; avoiding them lets it reset back up.
caveat: This means running a little higher for a while; that's expected and okay.
sources: Adam Brown / diaTribe, 'Bright Spots & Landmines' (free book), 2017, https://diatribe.org/bright-spots-and-landmines
Dexcom Canada FAQ, 'How could I prevent nighttime lows with earlier alerts?', https://www.dexcom.com/en-ca/faqs/g7/how-could-i-prevent-nighttime-lows-with-earlier-alerts

title: Avoiding overtreatment of lows
advice: It's really common to keep eating during a low because you still feel awful - the symptoms often last after glucose has started rising. Overtreating then leads to a rebound high and sometimes a correction that causes the next low.
how: Pre-measure your 15 g so you stop there. Set a 15-minute timer and wait it out (sit down, drink water). Use your CGM arrow: if it's turning up, give it more time. If you rebound high after treating, don't rush a correction - talk to your team about a plan.
why: Glucose absorption takes 10-15 minutes and adrenaline symptoms linger, so extra eating stacks carbs that all arrive later.
sources: Diabetes Canada CPG Ch.14 Hypoglycemia, 2018, https://guidelines.diabetes.ca/cpg/chapter14
ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026, Section 6 Glycemic Goals and Hypoglycemia, 2026, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc26-S006

title: Don't eat until you feel better
advice: The shaky, hungry feeling lasts longer than the low itself, so eating until it passes nearly always sends you high. Take the measured amount, then sit it out for 15 minutes.
how: Take a fixed 15-20 g and set a 15-minute timer. Re-check with a fingerstick or watch the CGM trend arrow; the CGM lags blood by about 5-15 minutes. Repeat only if you're still below 4.0. A flat or upward arrow means the treatment is working, even while the number still looks low.
why: Adrenaline and symptoms linger after glucose has started to rise, and the extra food on top of the hormonal (counter-regulatory) rise drives a rebound high.
sources: Diabetes Canada CPG Ch. 14 Hypoglycemia, 2018, https://www.diabetes.ca/for-professionals/full-guidelines/chapter-14
ADA Standards of Care 2026, Sec. 6, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc26-S006

title: Bagels are bigger than they look
advice: A lot of people are surprised that a big bakery or coffee-shop bagel can carry 50-60 g of carbs or more - about the same as three or four slices of bread. That's one of the most common sources of a morning spike.
how: Check the nutrition info for your usual brand (Tim Hortons, grocery-store, Montreal-style vary a lot). Options: half a bagel with an egg or peanut butter, a thin/mini bagel, or a whole-grain version. Pairing with protein (egg, smoked salmon) can soften the rise.
why: Bagels are dense, low-fibre refined starch that digests quickly, so the carbs hit fast and in a large amount.
sources: Tim Hortons Canada. Nutrition & Allergens, n.d., https://www.timhortons.ca/nutrition-and-allergens
Health Canada. Canadian Nutrient File, n.d., https://food-nutrition.canada.ca/cnf-fce/

title: The overnight basal check (flat-line test)
advice: Educators use a simple test to see whether the long-acting is right: a clean night with no late food or correction, and see whether your line stays flat. If it falls a lot, the long-acting is probably strong. If it climbs, it may be weak.
how: Eat supper early (finish by about 18:00-19:00) and keep it low in fat. No snacks after it and no correction insulin after supper. Go to bed in range (not low), and don't do it after a day of exercise or alcohol, or while sick. Watch the CGM from about 4 hours after the supper bolus until breakfast. A change of more than about 1.5-2 mmol/L up or down overnight suggests the basal needs looking at. Repeat on 2-3 nights before drawing a conclusion. If you go below 4.0, stop the test and treat the low; that itself is the answer. Share the results with your team rather than adjusting on your own.
why: Removing food and rapid insulin isolates the effect of the basal insulin, so the shape of the line shows whether basal matches what the liver releases overnight.
sources: Holt RIG et al., ADA/EASD T1D Consensus, Diabetes Care 2021, https://doi.org/10.2337/dci21-0043
Diabetes Canada CPG Ch. 12 Glycemic Management in Adults with T1D, 2018, https://www.diabetes.ca/for-professionals/full-guidelines/chapter-12

title: Do a simple overnight basal check
advice: Before changing anything, a clean overnight test tells you whether your long-acting dose is right.
how: Eat an early, simple, low-fat dinner (by 6 p.m.), no snacks or corrections after, and watch the G7 overnight. Ideally you stay within about 1.5-2 mmol/L of where you went to bed. Repeat on 2-3 nights; stop and treat if you go under 4.
why: Removing food and rapid insulin isolates what the background insulin is doing.
caveat: Don't do it while sick, after a hard workout day, or after drinking.
sources: Gary Scheiner, 'Think Like a Pancreas' (book, 3rd ed.), 2020 (basal testing, exercise and meal-dosing chapters)

Juicebox Podcast (Scott Benner), 'Type 1 Diabetes Pro Tips' series: Pre Bolus, Bump and Nudge (#34, #44), Setting Basal Insulin (#37), Fat and Protein (#39), https://podbay.fm/p/type-1-diabetes-pro-tips
Diabetes UK Forum, 'Splitting Lantus dose' thread, https://forum.diabetes.org.uk/boards/threads/splitting-lantus-dose.15061

title: When you take the long-acting matters
advice: Long-acting insulins aren't perfectly flat, and the timing of the dose can put more of its effect overnight or in the morning. If your lows cluster at one time of day, ask your team whether moving the dose or splitting it would help.
how: Take it at the same time every day; set a phone alarm. If you take it at bedtime and the lows are in the early morning, or you take it in the morning and the lows are late morning to midday, mention that pattern. Your team may suggest moving or splitting the dose. Don't move it by more than an hour or two on your own without a plan, because you can end up with overlap or a gap.
why: Glargine U100 and detemir can have a mild peak and may last less than 24 hours in some people, which puts more effect at certain times.
sources: Holt RIG et al., ADA/EASD T1D Consensus, Diabetes Care 2021, https://doi.org/10.2337/dci21-0043

title: Is it the long-acting or the mealtime insulin?
advice: A simple rule: problems that show up overnight or long after a meal point to the long-acting. Problems in the 1-4 hours after eating point to the mealtime dose, its timing, or the carb count.
how: Basal window: overnight, and any stretch 4-5 hours or more after the last rapid dose with no food. Bolus window: 1-4 hours after a meal or correction. Look for the same thing happening at the same time on 3 or more days out of 14. Rough guide: a low 1-3 hours after a meal means the meal dose was too strong for that meal or the pre-bolus was too long. A high 1-2 hours after a meal that comes back to target means a timing issue. Still high 4 hours later means too little meal insulin or a fatty meal. Change one thing at a time, then wait several days before judging it.
why: Rapid insulin peaks at about 1-2 hours and is mostly gone by 4-5 hours, so the timing of a problem tells you which insulin is responsible.
sources: Holt RIG et al., ADA/EASD T1D Consensus, Diabetes Care 2021, https://doi.org/10.2337/dci21-0043
Danne T et al., International Consensus on Use of CGM, Diabetes Care 2017, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc17-1600

title: Bedtime check and a bedtime snack
advice: Look at your Dexcom before bed every night. If you're on the low side, or drifting down, have a small snack with some protein before you sleep. That's a short-term safety net while your team sorts out the bigger fix.
how: Many educators suggest a snack of about 15 g of carbs with protein (for example toast with peanut butter, or crackers and cheese) when bedtime glucose is below about 7 mmol/L, falling, or after exercise or alcohol that day. Don't take bolus insulin for a snack whose purpose is preventing a low. Diabetes Canada recommends more checks, including some during sleep, for people with nocturnal lows. If you're having snacks every night just to stay safe, tell your team: it means the insulin needs adjusting.
why: Slowly digested carbs with protein bridge the hours when basal insulin and any remaining meal insulin outpace the body's needs.
sources: Diabetes Canada CPG Ch. 14 Hypoglycemia, Rec. 3.3, 2018, https://www.diabetes.ca/for-professionals/full-guidelines/chapter-14
ADA Standards of Care 2026, Sec. 6, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc26-S006

title: Good bedtime snack choices
advice: If you do have a bedtime snack, pick something that releases slowly rather than something sugary. Slow carb plus a bit of protein or fat tends to last longer through the night.
how: Ideas with about 15-20 g carb: 1 slice whole-grain toast with peanut butter; 3/4 cup plain Greek yogurt with berries; 4-6 whole-grain crackers with cheese; a cup of milk with a few almonds; half an apple with peanut butter.
why: Fibre, fat and protein slow digestion so the glucose arrives gradually over a few hours instead of all at once.
sources: Kalergis M et al. Optimizing insulin delivery: role of bedtime snacks in nocturnal hypoglycemia in T1D (cornstarch vs standard snack). Diabetes Care, 2003, https://doi.org/10.2337/diacare.26.1.9
ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines 2022: Nutritional management in children and adolescents with diabetes (Annan et al.), 2022, https://www.ispad.org/page/ISPADGuidelines2022

title: Bedtime snacks: what the evidence says
advice: Research on routine bedtime snacks in T1D is mixed - some studies show fewer overnight lows, others show no benefit and some higher mornings. They're a tool for certain nights, not a requirement.
how: A bedtime snack tends to make sense when: glucose is under about 7 mmol/L at bed with insulin still active, after exercise in the afternoon or evening, or after alcohol. Otherwise, many people do fine without one.
why: Slow carb plus protein provides glucose over several hours, but routine use adds calories and can mask an insulin mismatch.
sources: Raju B et al. Nocturnal hypoglycemia in type 1 diabetes: an assessment of preventive bedtime treatments. J Clin Endocrinol Metab, 2006, https://academic.oup.com/jcem/article/91/6/2087/2843397
Kalergis M et al. Optimizing insulin delivery: role of bedtime snacks in nocturnal hypoglycemia in T1D (cornstarch vs standard snack). Diabetes Care, 2003, https://doi.org/10.2337/diacare.26.1.9
Axelsen M et al. Nocturnal glycaemic decline prevented by bedtime uncooked cornstarch in T1D. Diabet Med, 1999, https://gupea.ub.gu.se/handle/2077/12841

title: If you need a snack every night, it's probably the insulin
advice: Snacking to stay safe is fine on occasion, but if it's every night, the overnight insulin is likely a bit strong for you. That's worth fixing at the source.
how: Look at 3-4 nights where you didn't eat after dinner. If you drop more than ~1.5-2 mmol/L from bedtime to waking (or from 3 hours after dinner to 3 a.m.) with no food, bring that pattern to your diabetes team.
why: A steady overnight fall without food or recent rapid insulin points to basal being more than you need.
sources: Diabetes UK Forum, 'Bedtime snacks for type 1 diabetic', https://forum.diabetes.org.uk/boards/threads/bedtime-snacks-for-type-1-diabetic.114875
Gary Scheiner, 'Think Like a Pancreas' (book, 3rd ed.), 2020 (basal testing, exercise and meal-dosing chapters)
Diabetes UK Forum, 'Basal insulin at night' thread, https://forum.diabetes.org.uk/boards/threads/basal-insulin-at-night.94866/latest

title: A protein-plus-slow-carb snack when bedtime is lowish
advice: If you go to bed below about 7 and tend to drift down overnight, a small snack with protein and slow carbs is a classic, low-effort guard.
how: Ideas people swear by: a slice of seeded/whole-grain toast with peanut butter, peanut butter on 4-5 crackers (~15 g carbs), Greek yogurt, an apple with peanut butter, a glass of milk with a couple of plain cookies, half a banana, oatcakes. Many use a threshold: snack if under ~7.0 at bed, no snack if over 8.
why: Protein and fat slow absorption so the sugar trickles in over hours, matching a slow overnight drop.
caveat: An uncovered snack night after night is a bandage. If you need one every night, the basal or dinner dose likely needs a look with your team.
sources: Diabetes UK Forum, 'Bedtime snacks for type 1 diabetic', https://forum.diabetes.org.uk/boards/threads/bedtime-snacks-for-type-1-diabetic.114875
Breakthrough T1D Forum, 'Tips for night time snacks', https://forum.breakthrought1d.org/t/tips-for-night-time-snacks/74280
Gluroo blog, '10 Bedtime Snack Ideas for Type 1 Diabetes', https://gluroo.com/blog/nutrition/bedtime-snack-ideas-type-1-diabetes/

title: If you're not sure you'll finish the meal, dose after
advice: If you're dropping before a meal, or not sure how much you'll eat (restaurant, a dinner party), it's okay to inject after you see what you actually ate.
how: Inject as you finish, for what you ate. Fiasp/Lyumjev users often do this routinely.
why: Dosing for food not eaten is a main cause of post-meal lows.
caveat: Expect a larger spike than with a pre-bolus.
sources: Diabetes UK Forum, 'Swapping to Lyumjev from NovoRapid - your experiences please', https://forum.diabetes.org.uk/boards/threads/swapping-to-lyumjev-from-novor-your-experiences-please.118180/latest
diaTribe, 'Pizza and Blood Sugar Control: (Not Quite) Easy as Pie', https://diatribe.org/diet-and-nutrition/pizza-and-blood-sugar-control-not-quite-easy-pie

title: Why breakfast is often the hardest meal
advice: Lots of people with T1D find breakfast spikes the most, even with the same carbs as lunch. That's because the body is more insulin-resistant in the morning from overnight hormones - it's biology, not willpower.
how: Options that often help: a lower-carb or higher-protein breakfast (eggs, Greek yogurt, peanut butter on whole-grain toast), avoiding juice and sweetened cereals in the morning, longer pre-bolus time. If mornings are consistently harder, your team may suggest a different insulin-to-carb ratio for breakfast.
why: Cortisol and growth hormone rise in the early morning (dawn phenomenon), increasing insulin resistance for several hours.
sources: Porcellati F et al. Pathophysiology of the dawn phenomenon / morning insulin resistance in T1D. Diabetes Care, 2013, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=Porcellati+dawn+phenomenon+type+1+diabetes
ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines 2022: Nutritional management in children and adolescents with diabetes (Annan et al.), 2022, https://www.ispad.org/page/ISPADGuidelines2022

title: Burnout: focus on one small thing
advice: After 30 years, being tired of diabetes is normal. Picking just one thing to work on makes it manageable.
how: Pick one pattern (e.g., overnight lows) and work on it for 2 weeks; ignore the rest. Adam Brown's 'Bright Spots': notice what's working and do more of it.
why: Small achievable goals reduce overwhelm.
caveat: If feelings of hopelessness last more than two weeks, talk to your care team.
sources: Adam Brown / diaTribe, 'Bright Spots & Landmines' (free book), 2017, https://diatribe.org/bright-spots-and-landmines
CDC, '10 Tips for Coping with Diabetes Distress', https://www.cdc.gov/diabetes/articles/10-tips-coping-diabetes-distress.html
NDSS (Australia), 'Diabetes distress and burnout', https://www.ndss.com.au/looking-after-your-mind/when-diabetes-makes-it-tough/diabetes-distress-and-burnout/

title: Tell your care team how you feel
advice: Diabetes distress is common and treatable. Your diabetes educator or doctor wants to hear about it.
how: Mention it at your next appointment, or ask for a referral to a psychologist or social worker familiar with diabetes; in Canada, Diabetes Canada and Breakthrough T1D Canada have peer-support programs.
why: Distress is linked to worse glucose outcomes; support helps both.
sources: CDC, '10 Tips for Coping with Diabetes Distress', https://www.cdc.gov/diabetes/articles/10-tips-coping-diabetes-distress.html
NDSS (Australia), 'Diabetes distress and burnout', https://www.ndss.com.au/looking-after-your-mind/when-diabetes-makes-it-tough/diabetes-distress-and-burnout/

title: How accurate does carb counting need to be?
advice: Being within about 10 g of a meal's true carbs usually doesn't make a big difference, but misses of 20 g or more often do. Adults with T1D tend to overestimate some foods and underestimate others, and bigger errors are linked to more glucose swings.
how: Focus your accuracy effort on the big carb items (bagels, pizza crust, nachos, rice, pasta, sweet drinks) rather than small extras. If lows after a particular meal keep happening, re-check that meal's carb estimate first - it's often overestimated.
why: Errors scale with portion size, so the largest carb sources produce the largest insulin-to-carb mismatches.
sources: Brazeau AS et al. Carbohydrate counting accuracy and blood glucose variability in adults with type 1 diabetes. Diabetes Res Clin Pract, 2013, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.diabres.2012.10.024

Smart CE et al. Can children with type 1 diabetes and their caregivers estimate the carbohydrate content of meals and snacks? / carb-estimation error of 10 g vs 20 g. Diabet Med, 2009-2010, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=Smart+CE+carbohydrate+counting+accuracy+type+1

title: Carb counting: close is good enough
advice: You don't have to be perfect. Being within about 10 grams per meal is usually fine. Over-estimating carbs is a common hidden cause of after-meal lows.
how: Re-check the counts for meals you eat often (weigh them once or twice, or use the label). A refresher with a dietitian helps after years of estimating. If a particular meal keeps dropping you low, recount it before blaming the ratio.
why: Studies show that errors of about ±10 g per meal usually stay within target, while bigger errors cause predictable highs or lows.
sources: Smart CE et al., Children and adolescents on intensive insulin therapy maintain postprandial glycaemic control without precise carbohydrate counting, Diabet Med 2009, https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1464-5491.2009.02669.x
Diabetes Canada CPG Ch. 11 Nutrition Therapy, 2018, https://www.diabetes.ca/for-professionals/full-guidelines/chapter-11

title: Carb counting is the core skill on MDI
advice: On injections, carb counting is what lets you eat flexibly - so it's worth a periodic tune-up, even after 30 years. People often find their 'eyeball' estimates have drifted over time, especially for restaurant food.
how: Once or twice a year, weigh or measure your usual foods for a week (your cereal bowl, bagel, pasta portion) and compare with your estimates. Read the 'Total carbohydrate' line on Canadian labels and check the serving size against what you actually eat.
why: Mealtime insulin is matched to carbohydrate, so an under- or over-estimate shows up directly as a post-meal high or low.
sources: Evert AB et al. Nutrition Therapy for Adults With Diabetes or Prediabetes: A Consensus Report. Diabetes Care, 2019, https://doi.org/10.2337/dci19-0014
Diabetes Canada CPG Ch.11 Nutrition Therapy (Sievenpiper et al.), 2018, https://guidelines.diabetes.ca/cpg/chapter11
ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026, Section 5 Facilitating Positive Health Behaviors, 2026, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc26-S005

title: Set your Dexcom alerts to catch lows early
advice: Your Dexcom can warn you before you're actually low, which matters most at night. Set the low alert higher than 3.9, and make sure the alarms are loud enough to wake you.
how: In the G7 app: set the Low alert at 4.4 mmol/L or higher (the exercise consensus suggests 4.4 overnight, higher if you're at elevated risk, for example 5.0-5.6 after exercise or alcohol). Keep the 'Urgent Low Soon' alert on; it warns about 20 minutes before reaching 3.1. Turn on the falling rate alert. Check that the phone isn't on Do Not Disturb silencing alerts, and keep it near the bed. Consider Dexcom Follow so a partner gets the alerts too. When the low alert sounds with a down arrow, a small snack of 10-15 g can head the low off.
why: An earlier alert gives a window to eat before going below 3.0, and lows that sit for hours usually mean the alarm wasn't heard or acted on.
sources: Moser O et al., EASD/ISPAD position statement on exercise with CGM, Diabetologia 2020, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00125-020-05263-9
ADA Standards of Care 2026, Sec. 7 Diabetes Technology, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc26-S007

title: When to double-check the Dexcom with a fingerstick
advice: Your Dexcom is very good, but check with a fingerstick when the reading doesn't match how you feel, during the first day of a new sensor, or while glucose is changing fast.
how: Do a fingerstick when symptoms don't match the reading, on sensor day 1, after a compression-type drop, or before driving if the reading is borderline. Dexcom can be calibrated in the app if it's consistently off. CGM lags blood by about 5-15 minutes, more during rapid change or exercise.
why: Interstitial fluid glucose trails blood glucose, especially when levels are changing rapidly.
sources: ADA Standards of Care 2026, Sec. 7, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc26-S007
Diabetes Canada CPG Ch. 9 Monitoring Glycemic Control, 2018, https://www.diabetes.ca/for-professionals/full-guidelines/chapter-9

title: Using your CGM to learn your foods
advice: Your CGM is a great tool for learning how your favourite foods behave - not to judge, just to understand. Many people find it really eye-opening.
how: Pick one meal you eat often. For 3 times, record the carb estimate, dose time, and CGM at 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 hours. Look for patterns: early dip? late rise? Share with your team. Most CGM apps let you add meal notes.
why: Repeated observations show your personal response, which can differ from general averages.
sources: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026, Section 6 Glycemic Goals and Hypoglycemia, 2026, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc26-S006
Bell KJ et al. Impact of Fat, Protein, and Glycemic Index on Postprandial Glucose Control in Type 1 Diabetes. Diabetes Care, 2015, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc15-0100

title: The CGM targets that matter
advice: The international targets are more than 70% of the time between 3.9 and 10, less than 4% of the time below 3.9 and less than 1% below 3.0. Your lows are the number to work on first. Bringing them down usually helps everything else too.
how: Targets for most adults with T1D: time in range (3.9-10.0 mmol/L) above 70% (about 17 h/day); time below 3.9 under 4% (under 1 h/day); time below 3.0 under 1% (under 15 min/day); time above 10.0 under 25%; time above 13.9 under 5%; CV 36% or less. Judge them on at least 14 days of data with the sensor worn 70% or more of the time. For people at high risk of hypoglycemia, the consensus loosens the goals to time in range above 50% and time below 3.9 under 1%. Every 5% gain in time in range is clinically meaningful.
why: Time below range is the metric most directly tied to immediate danger, so the consensus treats cutting it as the first priority, ahead of raising time in range.
sources: Battelino T et al., Clinical Targets for CGM Data Interpretation: International Consensus on Time in Range, Diabetes Care 2019, https://doi.org/10.2337/dci19-0028
ADA Standards of Care 2026, Sec. 6 Glycemic Goals, Hypoglycemia, and Hyperglycemic Crises, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc26-S006

title: Change one thing at a time
advice: It works best to fix one pattern at a time, overnight first, then each meal, and give each change a few days before judging it. Lots of changes at once make it impossible to tell what worked.
how: Order clinicians use: 1) stop the lows, especially overnight; 2) get fasting and overnight steady (basal); 3) then meals, one at a time; 4) then the variability. After any change agreed with your team, wait about 3-7 days before judging it. Review a 14-day AGP every 2-4 weeks.
why: Basal changes take 2-3 days to settle, and day-to-day noise hides the effect of any single change.
sources: Danne T et al., International Consensus on Use of CGM, Diabetes Care 2017, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc17-1600
Holt RIG et al., ADA/EASD T1D Consensus, Diabetes Care 2021, https://doi.org/10.2337/dci21-0043

title: Late lows can be the dinner shot, not the basal
advice: Lows in the first half of the night are often the tail end of the dinner insulin, especially after a late dinner or an evening walk.
how: Notice timing: a low 2-5 hours after dinner points to the meal dose or ratio; a low at 3-6 a.m. with nothing eaten after 8 p.m. points more to basal. Some people eat dinner earlier, or reduce the dinner dose on nights with an after-dinner walk (discuss with your team).
why: Rapid insulin acts for 4-5 hours, so a 7 p.m. dinner shot can still be working at midnight.
sources: Diabetes UK Forum, 'Bedtime snacks for type 1 diabetic', https://forum.diabetes.org.uk/boards/threads/bedtime-snacks-for-type-1-diabetic.114875
Breakthrough T1D Forum, 'Tips for night time snacks', https://forum.breakthrought1d.org/t/tips-for-night-time-snacks/74280

title: Chicken burger and fries
advice: A crispy chicken burger is a carb-and-fat combo: the bun and breading both count, and fries add a lot. It's a meal where a late rise is common.
how: Rough guide: bun 25-35 g carbs, breaded chicken patty 10-25 g, small fries 30-40 g, medium 45-55 g. Check the restaurant's online nutrition info. Grilled chicken, a side salad or swapping half the fries for veg can lower the load.
why: Breading and bun are refined starch, and frying fat slows absorption, combining a fast and delayed rise.
sources: CalorieKing food database, n.d., https://www.calorieking.com
Bell KJ et al. Impact of Fat, Protein, and Glycemic Index on Postprandial Glucose Control in Type 1 Diabetes. Diabetes Care, 2015, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc15-0100

title: Coffee and caffeine
advice: Black coffee has almost no carbs, but some people with T1D see a modest rise after it, especially in the morning. Caffeine can also make low symptoms feel stronger - which can be a helpful warning sign.
how: Test it yourself: try black or unsweetened coffee on a few mornings without food and watch the CGM for 2 hours. If you see a consistent bump, mention it to your team. Remember: the carbs in coffee come from milk, cream, sugar and syrups.
why: Caffeine raises adrenaline and can reduce insulin sensitivity short-term, and it heightens adrenergic hypo symptoms.
sources: Watson JM et al. Influence of caffeine on the frequency and perception of hypoglycemia in free-living patients with type 1 diabetes. Diabetes Care, 2000, https://doi.org/10.2337/diacare.23.4.455

title: Coffee shop drinks carbs
advice: Specialty coffees can hold more carbs than a meal - an Iced Capp or flavoured latte can be 40-70 g. A plain coffee with milk is a whole different story.
how: Tim Hortons medium Double Double is roughly 20-25 g carbs (mostly sugar); a medium Iced Capp is around 50-60 g. Check the Tim Hortons nutrition calculator for your exact order. Lower-carb choices: 'Double-Double' made with sweetener instead of sugar, plain latte, or an Americano with milk.
why: Liquid sugars absorb quickly with nothing to slow them, producing a sharp rise.
sources: Tim Hortons Canada. Nutrition & Allergens, n.d., https://www.timhortons.ca/nutrition-and-allergens

title: Black coffee can push some people up
advice: Even black coffee can nudge sugar up for some people. Watch your own graph; it varies a lot.
how: Check the G7 for an hour after coffee on a few no-breakfast mornings. If you rise, people either have coffee with breakfast so it's covered, or include it in their breakfast dose planning.
why: Caffeine raises adrenaline and can cause short-term insulin resistance.
caveat: A latte has milk carbs (~12 g per cup of milk) that need counting.
sources: T1D Exchange, 'What We Learned from the Online Community in August' (compression-low, alcohol-wipe and zero-sugar polls), 2022, https://t1dexchange.org/articles/top-questions-of-the-day-august-2022
TCOYD, 'How to Treat Foot to Floor Phenomenon', 2020, https://tcoyd.org/2020/07/how-to-manage-foot-to-floor-phenomenon/
Diabetes UK Forum, 'Morning spike in sugars', https://forum.diabetes.org.uk/boards/threads/morning-spike-in-sugars.96658/latest

title: Spot compression lows from lying on the sensor
advice: Some 'lows' at night aren't real. If you sleep on your sensor, the pressure can make the G7 read falsely low.
how: Tell-tale shape: a sudden straight drop, then a quick bounce back up when you roll over. Check with a finger prick before treating. Wear the sensor on the side you don't sleep on, high on the back of the arm, or try the upper buttock/abdomen if you're a side-sleeper.
why: Pressure squeezes fluid away from the sensor wire for 15-20 minutes, so it reads low.
caveat: A slow steady fall is more likely a true low; treat it.
sources: T1D Exchange, 'What We Learned from the Online Community in August' (compression-low, alcohol-wipe and zero-sugar polls), 2022, https://t1dexchange.org/articles/top-questions-of-the-day-august-2022
Diabetes UK Forum, 'Compression lows on Dexcom G7 vs Libre 3', https://forum.diabetes.org.uk/boards/threads/compression-lows-on-dexcom-g7-vs-libre-3.118389
Diabetes UK Forum, 'Compression lows', https://forum.diabetes.org.uk/boards/threads/compression-lows.113122
Diabetes UK Forum, 'Bedtime snacks for type 1 diabetic', https://forum.diabetes.org.uk/boards/threads/bedtime-snacks-for-type-1-diabetic.114875

title: Is that night-time low real? Compression lows
advice: Sometimes lying on the sensor arm makes the Dexcom show a sudden steep drop that isn't real. A fingerstick tells the difference. Still, a low that lasts for hours is more likely to be genuine.
how: Signs of a compression artifact: a sudden, very steep drop at night while you were lying on the sensor side, then a sharp bounce back up when you roll over, and no symptoms. If you're unsure, check a fingerstick before treating. Try placing the sensor where you won't lie on it. Don't brush off slow, long-lasting lows as compression; treat and report them.
why: Pressure on the sensor site reduces blood flow to the tissue around it, which lowers the glucose the sensor reads.
sources: ADA Standards of Care 2026, Sec. 7 Diabetes Technology, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc26-S007
Diabetes Canada CPG Ch. 9 Monitoring Glycemic Control, 2018, https://www.diabetes.ca/for-professionals/full-guidelines/chapter-9

title: Uncooked cornstarch snacks
advice: Uncooked cornstarch is a very slowly digested starch that some people use to cover the overnight hours. Studies are small and mixed, so it's something to discuss with your team rather than a first choice.
how: Some specialty bars containing uncooked cornstarch are sold for this purpose. Ask your diabetes educator before trying one, and watch your CGM closely on the first few nights for morning highs.
why: Raw cornstarch is digested over 6 or more hours, releasing glucose slowly through the night.
sources: Axelsen M et al. Nocturnal glycaemic decline prevented by bedtime uncooked cornstarch in T1D. Diabet Med, 1999, https://gupea.ub.gu.se/handle/2077/12841
Kalergis M et al. Optimizing insulin delivery: role of bedtime snacks in nocturnal hypoglycemia in T1D (cornstarch vs standard snack). Diabetes Care, 2003, https://doi.org/10.2337/diacare.26.1.9
Raju B et al. Nocturnal hypoglycemia in type 1 diabetes: an assessment of preventive bedtime treatments. J Clin Endocrinol Metab, 2006, https://academic.oup.com/jcem/article/91/6/2087/2843397

title: Choosing creamer and milk
advice: Creamers vary a lot: plain cream has almost no carbs, while flavoured creamers and oat milk add sugar quickly. Small swaps can lower morning carbs without giving up your coffee.
how: Per tablespoon: 10% or 18% cream ~1 g, flavoured coffee creamer ~5-6 g, milk ~0.75 g; per cup, oat milk barista ~15-20 g vs. unsweetened almond ~1 g. Measuring your pour once or twice helps make dosing more reliable.
why: Lactose and added sugars are the carb source; fat in cream contributes almost none.
sources: Health Canada. Canadian Nutrient File, n.d., https://food-nutrition.canada.ca/cnf-fce/

title: High in the morning: dawn effect, or rebound after a night low?
advice: A steady climb from about 3 or 4 a.m. with no low before it is the dawn effect, from natural morning hormones. A morning high after a night-time low is usually from treating the low or from rebound. Either way, the fix starts with stopping the night lows, not taking more insulin.
how: Look at the overnight CGM trace. Flat, then rising from about 03:00-08:00 means dawn phenomenon; a basal timing or type change may help (team decision). A low followed by a high means over-treatment or counter-regulation, so prevent the low. CGM studies show that nocturnal lows are usually followed by normal or low fasting glucose, not highs, so the classic 'Somogyi effect' is uncommon. Don't raise the long-acting for morning highs if there were lows overnight.
why: Growth hormone and cortisol rise before waking and increase insulin resistance, while a true night low is usually followed by low or normal fasting glucose.
sources: Hoi-Hansen T, Pedersen-Bjergaard U, Thorsteinsson B, The Somogyi phenomenon revisited using CGM in daily life, Diabetologia 2005, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=Somogyi+phenomenon+revisited+continuous+glucose+monitoring+Hoi-Hansen
Holt RIG et al., ADA/EASD T1D Consensus, Diabetes Care 2021, https://doi.org/10.2337/dci21-0043

title: Diabetes fatigue and fear of lows are real
advice: Thirty years of daily decisions is a lot, and frequent lows, especially at night, are frightening and exhausting. Feeling worn down is normal and worth telling your team about. It's part of diabetes care, not a failing.
how: ADA recommends screening for diabetes distress and fear of hypoglycemia, and referral for support when needed. Ask your clinic about a social worker or psychologist with diabetes experience, or Diabetes Canada peer support. Practical relief: let tools do some of the work (CGM alerts, Dexcom Follow, asking about AID).
why: Distress and fear of lows lead to over-eating to stay safe, missed doses and rebounds, which make control harder.
sources: ADA Standards of Care 2026, Sec. 5, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc26-S005
Diabetes Canada CPG Ch. 18 Diabetes and Mental Health, 2018, https://www.diabetes.ca/for-professionals/full-guidelines/chapter-18

title: Never mute the night alarms when you live with lows
advice: After decades of type 1, the body's own low warnings often get quieter. The phone alarm is your safety net, so keep it loud.
how: Keep the phone charged on the nightstand (not in another room), check that Do Not Disturb doesn't silence Dexcom (it has an override), and keep volume up. Some people put the phone in a glass to amplify it.
why: Long-duration type 1 and repeated lows blunt adrenaline warning symptoms, so you may not wake on your own.
sources: Dexcom FAQ, 'How can I get fewer nighttime alerts with G7?', https://www.dexcom.com/en-us/faqs/how-can-i-get-fewer-nighttime-alerts
Beyond Type 1, 'Tip Sheet for Continuous Glucose Monitors', https://beyondtype1.org/tip-sheet-for-continuous-glucose-monitors-cgms

title: Above 5 to drive
advice: Check your Dexcom before you drive. Be above 5 and not dropping. If you go low, pull over, treat it, and wait until you've fully recovered before you drive again.
how: Diabetes Canada guidance: don't drive if glucose is below 4.0. Be above 5.0 before driving, and keep fast sugar in the car. After treating a low, wait about 40 minutes after recovery before driving, because thinking lags behind glucose. Check every few hours on long drives.
why: Reaction time and judgement are impaired during a low and for some time after it, even once the numbers have recovered.
sources: Diabetes Canada CPG Ch. 21 Diabetes and Driving, 2018, https://www.diabetes.ca/for-professionals/full-guidelines/chapter-21
Diabetes Canada CPG Ch. 14 Hypoglycemia, Rec. 2, 2018, https://www.diabetes.ca/for-professionals/full-guidelines/chapter-14

title: Have a few carbs before an unplanned walk
advice: If you're heading out for an unplanned walk or chore and have recently taken insulin, a few carbs beforehand is a simple safety step.
how: Rough guide from exercise researchers: 10-20 g before light activity if no recent mealtime insulin, 15-30 g if you injected in the last 2 hours. Bring tabs.
why: Active muscles plus active insulin pull sugar down fast.
sources: Baker Heart & Diabetes Institute fact sheet, 'Physical activity and type 1 diabetes', https://www.baker.edu.au/-/media/documents/fact-sheets/baker-institute_physical-activity-t1-diabetes.pdf
Riddell Lab, York University (Canada), 'Making Real-Time Insulin Adjustments', 2020, https://mriddell.lab.yorku.ca/files/2020/11/Making-Real-Time-Insulin-Adjustments.pdf

title: Snacks during exercise by trend arrow
advice: During exercise, use the arrow as well as the number. The faster you're falling, the more carbs you need, and the earlier you take them.
how: EASD/ISPAD CGM guidance for adults (moderate risk): at about 7.0 mmol/L with a flat arrow, 10-15 g of carbs; with a slight down arrow, 15-25 g; with a down arrow, 20-35 g. Repeat every 15-20 minutes if needed, and again if the reading hasn't risen within 30 minutes. For longer exercise: 30-60 g of carbs per hour.
why: CGM lags blood glucose during exercise, so the trend predicts where blood glucose is now better than the number alone.
sources: Moser O et al., EASD/ISPAD position statement, Diabetologia 2020, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00125-020-05263-9
Riddell MC et al., Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2017, https://doi.org/10.1016/S2213-8587(17)30014-1

title: Afternoon or evening exercise means a lower night
advice: Activity keeps working on your sugar for hours afterward. An afternoon of gardening or an evening walk often shows up as a 2 a.m. low.
how: On active days: have a bedtime snack even if in range, raise the overnight Low alert, and talk to your team about a lower dinner dose on those days.
why: Muscles refill their glycogen stores for up to 24 hours after activity, pulling sugar from the blood.
sources: Baker Heart & Diabetes Institute fact sheet, 'Physical activity and type 1 diabetes', https://www.baker.edu.au/-/media/documents/fact-sheets/baker-institute_physical-activity-t1-diabetes.pdf
Riddell Lab, York University (Canada), 'Making Real-Time Insulin Adjustments', 2020, https://mriddell.lab.yorku.ca/files/2020/11/Making-Real-Time-Insulin-Adjustments.pdf
Breakthrough T1D Forum, 'Tips for night time snacks', https://forum.breakthrought1d.org/t/tips-for-night-time-snacks/74280

title: Exercise lows can show up that night
advice: Afternoon or evening activity, including heavy gardening, a long walk or a busy day on your feet, can cause a low 6 to 15 hours later, often in the middle of the night. On those days, plan your bedtime ahead.
how: After afternoon or evening exercise: set the overnight low alert at 4.4 mmol/L or higher; have a carb-plus-protein bedtime snack; avoid bedtime corrections; at 4.4 overnight, take 10 g of carbs with a flat arrow or 15 g with a slight down arrow, and more if it's falling faster. For MDI, the consensus mentions trimming the basal on heavy-activity days; ask your team whether and how much.
why: Muscles keep refilling their glycogen stores and stay more sensitive to insulin for up to about 24 hours after exercise.
sources: Moser O et al., EASD/ISPAD position statement, Diabetologia 2020, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00125-020-05263-9
Riddell MC et al., Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2017, https://doi.org/10.1016/S2213-8587(17)30014-1

title: Where to be before exercise
advice: Before moderate exercise like a brisk walk, aim to start somewhere around 7 to 10. Below 5, have a snack and wait before starting.
how: Starting glucose: ideally 7.0-10.0 mmol/L; if you're at high risk of lows, the consensus suggests starting a bit higher. 5.0-6.9: have 10-20 g of carbs first, depending on the arrow. Below 5.0: take carbs and delay until you're at least 5.0 and rising. Above 15.0: check blood ketones; above 1.5 mmol/L, don't exercise. Stop exercising if you fall below about 4.4-5.0 during it, treat, and restart only once you're at least 5.0 with a flat or rising arrow. Never exercise below 3.0.
why: Working muscles take up glucose without needing insulin, and that adds to the insulin already circulating, so the starting level needs a buffer.
sources: Riddell MC et al., Exercise management in T1D: a consensus statement, Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2017, https://doi.org/10.1016/S2213-8587(17)30014-1
Moser O et al., EASD/ISPAD position statement, Diabetologia 2020, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00125-020-05263-9

title: Exercising after a meal: a lighter mealtime dose
advice: If you're going to be active within an hour or two after eating, the mealtime insulin for that meal is usually reduced. Ask your team for a personal 'exercise meal' rule.
how: The 2017 consensus suggests a reduced pre-exercise meal bolus, with the size of the reduction depending on how hard and how long the exercise is. Your team sets the amount. Exercising when there's a lot of rapid insulin on board (the first 90 minutes after a bolus) carries the highest risk of a low. Fasted morning exercise (before breakfast insulin) carries the lowest risk of a low.
why: Insulin from the meal dose peaks at the same time as the muscles' glucose uptake, so the two effects add together.
sources: Riddell MC et al., Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2017, https://doi.org/10.1016/S2213-8587(17)30014-1
ADA Standards of Care 2026, Sec. 5, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc26-S005

title: Lower the meal dose before planned activity
advice: If you know you'll be active within a couple of hours after eating, lowering that meal's dose is better than eating extra later.
how: Exercise guidelines give percentage reductions by intensity and timing; ask your team for your own starting point, then test it on a few walks with the G7 and tabs handy.
why: Activity increases insulin sensitivity, so the same dose works harder.
sources: Baker Heart & Diabetes Institute fact sheet, 'Physical activity and type 1 diabetes', https://www.baker.edu.au/-/media/documents/fact-sheets/baker-institute_physical-activity-t1-diabetes.pdf
Diabetes UK Forum, exercise bolus-reduction discussion, https://forum.diabetes.org.uk/boards/goto/post?id=439910
Riddell Lab, York University (Canada), 'Making Real-Time Insulin Adjustments', 2020, https://mriddell.lab.yorku.ca/files/2020/11/Making-Real-Time-Insulin-Adjustments.pdf

title: Snacks for activity
advice: Activity often lowers glucose during and for hours after, so carbs before or during can prevent lows. How much depends on timing and insulin on board.
how: For 30-60 minutes of moderate activity, many people take 15-30 g carbs before or during (banana, granola bar, juice). Check before, during and after. If activity regularly causes lows, ask your team about dose adjustments around exercise.
why: Muscle uses more glucose during exercise and stays more insulin-sensitive for up to 24 hours afterward.
sources: Riddell MC et al. Exercise management in type 1 diabetes: a consensus statement. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol, 2017, https://doi.org/10.1016/S2213-8587(17)30014-1

title: Exercise before breakfast is gentler on lows
advice: Morning activity before breakfast, when there's little mealtime insulin around, is usually less likely to cause lows than exercise right after a meal shot.
how: A morning walk before breakfast often keeps people steady or even slightly raises them. If you exercise after a meal, give it 1-2 hours after the shot or plan a lower meal dose with your team.
why: Little rapid insulin is active in the fasted state, and morning hormones raise glucose.
caveat: Hard or intense workouts can raise sugar briefly.
sources: Baker Heart & Diabetes Institute fact sheet, 'Physical activity and type 1 diabetes', https://www.baker.edu.au/-/media/documents/fact-sheets/baker-institute_physical-activity-t1-diabetes.pdf
Riddell Lab, York University (Canada), 'Making Real-Time Insulin Adjustments', 2020, https://mriddell.lab.yorku.ca/files/2020/11/Making-Real-Time-Insulin-Adjustments.pdf

title: Different exercise, different effect
advice: Steady activity like walking, cycling or swimming tends to drop sugar. Short intense bursts or weights can push it up for a while. Mixing the two can help balance things.
how: Doing resistance exercise before aerobic exercise, or adding a 10-second all-out sprint at the end, lowers the drop during and after exercise. A rise after intense exercise is usually temporary. Correct it cautiously (the 2020 statement suggests a reduced correction, and avoiding corrections near bedtime), because a late low can follow.
why: Intense effort releases adrenaline and cortisol, which push glucose out of the liver, while steady aerobic exercise mainly increases how much glucose the muscles use.
sources: Riddell MC et al., Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2017, https://doi.org/10.1016/S2213-8587(17)30014-1
Moser O et al., Diabetologia 2020, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00125-020-05263-9

title: Fiasp or Lyumjev for faster mealtime action
advice: Fiasp and Lyumjev act a bit faster than NovoRapid or Humalog, so some people find they spike less after meals and can inject closer to eating.
how: People switching report needing a shorter pre-bolus (often 0-10 minutes, but still ~20 min at breakfast for some), and some say they must eat promptly or they drop. Ask your doctor; both are available in Canada.
why: Additives (niacinamide, treprostinil) speed absorption from under the skin.
caveat: Some notice injection sting or that the speed seems to fade over months. Timing changes needed.
sources: Diabetes UK Forum, 'Swapping to Lyumjev from NovoRapid - your experiences please', https://forum.diabetes.org.uk/boards/threads/swapping-to-lyumjev-from-novor-your-experiences-please.118180/latest
Diabettech blog, 'Lyumjev: not as URLi as I expected', https://www.diabettech.com/insulin-lyumjev-not-as-urli-as-i-expected/

title: Why high-fat, high-protein meals rise late
advice: Fat and protein don't count as carbs, but in T1D they really do change the glucose curve: a rich meal often stays flat or even dips early, then rises 3-5 hours later. People often think their insulin 'didn't work' when it's really just mistimed.
how: Watch your CGM 3, 4 and 5 hours after a burger, pizza or nachos meal and note the pattern. If you consistently see an early dip then a late rise, bring 2-3 examples (screenshots) to your diabetes team.
why: Fat slows stomach emptying, and fat and protein both increase insulin needs later, so carbs arrive after rapid insulin has peaked.
sources: Bell KJ et al. Impact of Fat, Protein, and Glycemic Index on Postprandial Glucose Control in Type 1 Diabetes. Diabetes Care, 2015, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc15-0100

Smart CE et al. Both Dietary Protein and Fat Increase Postprandial Glucose Excursions in Children With Type 1 Diabetes, and the Effect Is Additive. Diabetes Care, 2013, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc13-0195
Paterson M et al. The Role of Dietary Protein and Fat in Glycaemic Control in Type 1 Diabetes. Curr Diab Rep, 2015, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4512569

title: Fat-protein units (FPU) - what they are
advice: Some clinics use 'fat-protein units' to estimate extra insulin for very rich meals, an approach from Polish researcher Ewa Pankowska. It tends to over-dose for many people, so most teams now use a modified, gentler version if at all.
how: If you're curious, ask your educator whether a fat-protein approach is right for you. The basic idea: 100 kcal from fat plus protein counts as one unit, but how it converts to insulin must be individualized by your team.
why: Each 100 kcal of fat and protein raises later glucose and insulin needs, but the original algorithm caused hypoglycemia in some studies.
sources: Pankowska E et al. Application of novel dual wave meal bolus (fat-protein units) in children with T1D. Pediatr Diabetes, 2009, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=Pankowska+dual+wave+bolus+fat+protein+units
ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines 2022: Nutritional management in children and adolescents with diabetes (Annan et al.), 2022, https://www.ispad.org/page/ISPADGuidelines2022
Bell KJ et al. Impact of Fat, Protein, and Glycemic Index on Postprandial Glucose Control in Type 1 Diabetes. Diabetes Care, 2015, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc15-0100

title: Fibre helps smooth glucose
advice: Diabetes Canada encourages people with diabetes to aim for more fibre - roughly 30-50 g a day - and most Canadians get about half that. Adding fibre gradually is one of the gentler ways to soften spikes.
how: Easy adds: a handful of berries, 1/2 cup beans or lentils in soup or chili, a side salad or veggies with pizza, ground flax in yogurt, whole-grain crackers. Increase slowly and drink water to avoid bloating.
why: Viscous (soluble) fibre slows stomach emptying and carb absorption, lowering the post-meal glucose peak.
sources: Diabetes Canada CPG Ch.11 Nutrition Therapy (Sievenpiper et al.), 2018, https://guidelines.diabetes.ca/cpg/chapter11
Evert AB et al. Nutrition Therapy for Adults With Diabetes or Prediabetes: A Consensus Report. Diabetes Care, 2019, https://doi.org/10.2337/dci19-0014

title: What 15 g looks like in Canadian foods
advice: It helps to know exactly what 15 g looks like so you don't guess under stress. Keep a pre-measured option in your bag, car and nightstand.
how: 15 g = 4 Dex4 tablets (4 g each, gives 16 g); 175 mL (3/4 cup) juice or regular pop; a small 125 mL juice box is ~14-16 g, a 200 mL box ~22-26 g; 1 tbsp (15 mL) honey or 3 sugar packets dissolved in water; 6 Life Savers; about 15 Skittles. Rockets (Smarties) vary by roll - check the wrapper.
why: These are mostly glucose, sucrose or fructose with no fat or protein, so they digest and absorb quickly.
sources: Diabetes Canada CPG Ch.14 Hypoglycemia, 2018, https://guidelines.diabetes.ca/cpg/chapter14
ADA Consumer Guide: Dex4 glucose tablets, 4 g carbohydrate each, n.d., https://consumerguide.diabetes.org/node/591

title: Confirm with a meter when the reading doesn't match how you feel
advice: If the Dexcom says low but you feel fine, or the drop looks oddly sharp, a quick finger prick can save you eating a few hundred calories you didn't need.
how: Keep a meter on the nightstand. For an overnight alarm with a sudden vertical drop, prick first; if the meter reads above 4.5, roll off the sensor and go back to sleep.
why: CGM can be off during rapid change and from pressure on the sensor; capillary blood is the ground truth.
caveat: If you feel low, treat first and check after; never delay treatment to test when symptomatic.
sources: diaTribe, 'Defeating the Hypoglycemia Binge', https://diatribe.org/diabetes-management/defeating-hypoglycemia-binge
Diabetes UK Forum, 'Compression lows', https://forum.diabetes.org.uk/boards/threads/compression-lows.113122
Diabetes UK Forum, 'Bedtime snacks for type 1 diabetic', https://forum.diabetes.org.uk/boards/threads/bedtime-snacks-for-type-1-diabetic.114875

title: Follow a low with a small snack if your next meal is hours away
advice: Once you're back up, if there's still a lot of the day or night ahead before you eat, a small slower snack keeps you from sliding right back down.
how: After the reading turns up past 4.0-4.5: a cheese string and a couple of crackers, half a slice of toast with peanut butter, or a small yogurt (about 10-15 g carbs with some protein).
why: Fast sugar is used up in 30-60 minutes; if active insulin or basal is still pushing down, you'll drop again.
caveat: Not needed if your next meal is within an hour; it can push you high.
sources: Healthline, 'Rule of 15 for diabetes', https://www.healthline.com/health/diabetes/rule-of-15-diabetes
Diabetes UK Forum, 'Bedtime snacks for type 1 diabetic', https://forum.diabetes.org.uk/boards/threads/bedtime-snacks-for-type-1-diabetic.114875

title: Apps for carb lookups
advice: Carb-counting apps save a lot of guesswork, especially for takeout and packaged foods. People often find one or two apps they trust and stick with.
how: CalorieKing (free, large restaurant database), Carb Manager, MyFitnessPal, and Health Canada's Canadian Nutrient File for basic foods. Many apps let you save your usual meals so you only look them up once. Crowd-entered entries can be wrong - prefer verified ones.
why: Using published data reduces carb-estimate error compared with eyeballing.
sources: CalorieKing food database, n.d., https://www.calorieking.com
Health Canada. Canadian Nutrient File, n.d., https://food-nutrition.canada.ca/cnf-fce/

title: Veggies and protein first, carbs last
advice: One simple thing that helps many people: eat the vegetables and protein part of the meal first, and the bread, rice or fries last. It doesn't change what you eat, just the order.
how: Start with the salad or veggies, then the protein, and finish with the starch about 10 minutes later. Even a side salad before pizza or a burger may help. Results vary - check your CGM to see if it works for you.
why: Fibre and protein eaten first slow stomach emptying and blunt the glucose peak from the carbs eaten after.
caveat: Studied mostly in type 2; in type 1 the slower rise can leave rapid insulin peaking early, so watch for a dip in the first hour.
sources: Shukla AP et al. Food Order Has a Significant Impact on Postprandial Glucose and Insulin Levels. Diabetes Care, 2015, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc15-0429

title: Match timing to food type
advice: Not every meal behaves the same. Fast carbs like cereal or a bagel rise quickly, while rich meals like pizza or nachos rise slowly - and a lot of after-meal lows come from early insulin meeting a slow meal.
how: Group your regular meals into 'fast' (cereal, toast with jam, bagel, sweet coffee) and 'slow' (pizza, burgers, creamy pasta). Note which give early lows or early spikes, and share the pattern with your team so they can tailor timing advice.
why: The speed of carb absorption varies with fat, fibre and processing, so the same carb count can peak at very different times.
sources: Bell KJ et al. Impact of Fat, Protein, and Glycemic Index on Postprandial Glucose Control in Type 1 Diabetes. Diabetes Care, 2015, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc15-0100
Cobry E et al. Timing of meal insulin boluses to achieve optimal postprandial glycemic control in patients with type 1 diabetes. Diabetes Technol Ther, 2010, https://doi.org/10.1089/dia.2009.0112

title: Getting up can kick off a morning rise
advice: Many people notice their sugar climbs as soon as they get out of bed, even without eating. It's common, and it's not your fault.
how: Community tactics on injections: take the breakfast shot before getting out of bed, or as soon as you wake, and wait before eating. Some take a small wake-up dose even if not eating (agree this with your team).
why: Morning stress hormones (cortisol, adrenaline) signal the liver to release sugar.
caveat: Don't do this on mornings you woke up low or near-low.
sources: TCOYD, 'How to Treat Foot to Floor Phenomenon', 2020, https://tcoyd.org/2020/07/how-to-manage-foot-to-floor-phenomenon/
Diabetes UK Forum, 'Morning spike in sugars', https://forum.diabetes.org.uk/boards/threads/morning-spike-in-sugars.96658/latest

title: Double-check the first day of a new G7
advice: The first day of a new sensor is often less accurate, and false lows overnight are common.
how: Many people insert the new sensor in the morning so the first night isn't the bumpy one, and confirm surprising readings with a finger prick.
why: The sensor needs time for the tissue to settle.
sources: Beyond Type 1, 'Tip Sheet for Continuous Glucose Monitors', https://beyondtype1.org/tip-sheet-for-continuous-glucose-monitors-cgms
Diabetes UK Forum, 'Compression lows', https://forum.diabetes.org.uk/boards/threads/compression-lows.113122

title: Early low, late high after meals? Ask about slow stomach emptying
advice: After many years of diabetes, some people's stomachs empty food slowly. The insulin then works before the food arrives, causing a low soon after eating and a high later. If you notice that pattern, or fullness, bloating or nausea, mention it to your doctor.
how: Pattern: a low or dip within 1-2 hours of eating, then a rise 3-5 hours later. Ask your doctor about gastroparesis screening (ADA covers it under neuropathy). Bolus timing tactics your team may suggest: injecting at the start of the meal or after it, or splitting the meal dose. Smaller, lower-fat meals empty faster.
why: Autonomic neuropathy from long-standing diabetes can slow how fast the stomach empties, which delays carb absorption relative to the insulin.
sources: ADA Standards of Care 2026, Sec. 12 Retinopathy, Neuropathy, and Foot Care, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc26-S012

title: Have glucagon and teach someone to use it
advice: With lows below 3.0 happening, you should have unexpired glucagon at home. The person you live with should know where it is and how to use it. Nasal Baqsimi is the easiest: it goes in one nostril, with no mixing and no needle.
how: ADA: prescribe glucagon for everyone on insulin who is at risk of level 2 or 3 lows, and teach family members. Diabetes Canada Rec. 9: teach support persons how to give glucagon. Baqsimi (3 mg nasal glucagon) has been approved in Canada since 2019; ask your pharmacist or doctor for a prescription. Give it when the person can't safely swallow or is unconscious, call 911, and turn them on their side. Check the expiry date. Glucagon works less well after more than 2 drinks of alcohol or a long fast.
why: Glucagon makes the liver release stored glucose, which raises blood sugar when the person can't eat.
sources: ADA Standards of Care 2026, Sec. 6, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc26-S006
Diabetes Canada CPG Ch. 14 Hypoglycemia, Rec. 7, 9, 2018, https://www.diabetes.ca/for-professionals/full-guidelines/chapter-14
Baqsimi Canadian Product Monograph (Eli Lilly / Amphastar), https://health-products.canada.ca/dpd-bdpp/ (search BAQSIMI)

title: Make sure your husband knows where the glucagon is
advice: With long-standing type 1 and frequent night lows, it's worth a quick refresh: does he know where the rescue glucagon is and how to use it?
how: Many people now carry nasal glucagon (Baqsimi) because it's a single puff with no mixing. Keep one in the bedroom and one in the bag; check expiry dates when daylight-saving changes.
why: Severe lows can stop you swallowing; glucagon makes the liver release stored sugar.
caveat: Glucagon works less well after heavy drinking because the liver is busy with alcohol.
sources: JDRF/Breakthrough T1D, 'Alcohol and Type 1 Diabetes: How to Manage a Night Out and the Morning After', https://www.jdrf.org/?p=138291
diaTribe, 'How to Coach Your Care-Partner on CGM Data', https://diatribe.org/lifestyle/how-coach-your-care-partner-cgm-data

title: Glycemic index in real life
advice: Glycemic index tells you how fast a carb food tends to raise glucose. It isn't about good or bad foods - it's about timing, so faster foods may need more lead time and slower ones less.
how: Swaps that often help: large-flake or steel-cut oats instead of instant, al dente pasta, parboiled or basmati rice, grainy breads, adding beans or lentils. Mixed meals with fat, protein and fibre lower the overall GI of the meal.
why: Lower-GI foods are digested and absorbed more slowly, flattening the post-meal peak so it better matches rapid insulin's action.
sources: Diabetes Canada CPG Ch.11 Nutrition Therapy (Sievenpiper et al.), 2018, https://guidelines.diabetes.ca/cpg/chapter11
Bell KJ et al. Impact of Fat, Protein, and Glycemic Index on Postprandial Glucose Control in Type 1 Diabetes. Diabetes Care, 2015, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc15-0100
University of Sydney Glycemic Index database, n.d., https://glycemicindex.com

title: Fruit gummies or jelly candies for gentler, longer lift
advice: Some people find straight glucose shoots them up then lets them drift back down. A few gummy fruit snacks give a slightly longer tail.
how: Common choices: fruit snacks (about 2-3 g each), jelly beans (~1 g each), Swedish Berries/Fish (~3-4 g each), Skittles (~1 g each, so 15 for 15 g). Count them out into small bags ahead of time.
why: Gelatin/starch candies digest a little slower than dextrose, smoothing the rise.
caveat: Chocolate and anything with fat (or diet versions) are too slow for a real low.
sources: Breakthrough T1D Forum, '15/15 rule outdated? If so, what is better way?', https://forum.breakthrought1d.org/t/15-15-rule-outdated-if-so-what-is-better-way/75173
Diabetes UK Forum, 'Bedtime snacks for type 1 diabetic', https://forum.diabetes.org.uk/boards/threads/bedtime-snacks-for-type-1-diabetic.114875

title: Pizza effect: fat and protein delay the rise
advice: Rich, fatty or high-protein meals like pizza, fries or a big restaurant supper often cause an early dip and then a high 3 to 6 hours later. The usual single shot before the meal doesn't fit that shape well.
how: Strategies your team may suggest for MDI: inject closer to the start of the meal, not with a long pre-bolus; split the meal dose into a part with the meal and a part 1-2 hours later; or plan a correction for the late rise. Don't stack a correction for the early rise. Watch for this pattern on restaurant nights.
why: Fat slows how fast the stomach empties and adds insulin resistance hours later, and protein adds some late glucose, so glucose peaks after rapid insulin has already peaked.
sources: Bell KJ et al., Impact of fat, protein, and glycemic index on postprandial glucose control in T1D, Diabetes Care 2015, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc15-0100

title: Hot showers, baths and saunas can speed insulin
advice: Heat brings blood to the skin, so recently injected insulin can hit faster. Some people see a drop during or after a hot bath or hot tub.
how: Avoid a long hot bath or sauna right after a meal shot; check the G7 before getting in; keep tabs nearby. Some see CGM rise after hot showers instead.
why: Heat increases skin blood flow, speeding absorption from under the skin.
caveat: Effects vary; some get a false high from the sensor warming.
sources: Diabetes Self-Management, 'Can People With Diabetes Safely Use Hot Tubs?', https://www.diabetesselfmanagement.com/healthy-living/general-health/can-people-with-diabetes-safely-use-hot-tubs/
Diabetes UK Forum, 'Insulin absorption factors', https://forum.diabetes.org.uk/boards/threads/insulin-absorption-factors.2739
Healthline, 'Do showers and baths affect blood sugars?', https://www.healthline.com/health/diabetes/do-showers-and-baths-affect-blood-sugars

title: Summer heat can bring more lows
advice: Many people find they need a little less insulin in hot weather and go low more easily.
how: Watch patterns in heat waves, keep hydrated, carry more low supplies.
why: Heat raises absorption and you're often more active.
sources: Diabetes UK Forum, 'Insulin absorption factors', https://forum.diabetes.org.uk/boards/threads/insulin-absorption-factors.2739
Diabetes Self-Management, 'Can People With Diabetes Safely Use Hot Tubs?', https://www.diabetesselfmanagement.com/healthy-living/general-health/can-people-with-diabetes-safely-use-hot-tubs/

title: Housework and shopping count as exercise
advice: Vacuuming, gardening, a big grocery trip, or walking around the mall all lower sugar just like 'real' exercise.
how: Treat a busy chore morning like a walk: carry tabs, maybe a few grams before starting if you injected recently.
why: Any muscle use increases glucose uptake.
sources: Baker Heart & Diabetes Institute fact sheet, 'Physical activity and type 1 diabetes', https://www.baker.edu.au/-/media/documents/fact-sheets/baker-institute_physical-activity-t1-diabetes.pdf
Adam Brown / diaTribe, 'Bright Spots & Landmines' (free book), 2017, https://diatribe.org/bright-spots-and-landmines

title: Hydration and glucose
advice: Water doesn't lower blood sugar directly, but being dehydrated can make highs worse and harder to bring down. Drinking water is a good habit, especially when glucose is high or you're unwell.
how: Aim for water with every meal and extra when glucose is above ~14 mmol/L. Choose water, sparkling water or diet drinks for everyday thirst. Sugary drinks are best saved for treating lows.
why: Dehydration concentrates glucose in the blood and reduces kidney excretion, while adequate fluid helps clear excess glucose.
sources: Diabetes Canada CPG Appendix 8: Sick-Day Medication List / Ch.15 Hyperglycemic emergencies, 2018, https://guidelines.diabetes.ca/cpg/chapter15
Diabetes Canada CPG Ch.11 Nutrition Therapy (Sievenpiper et al.), 2018, https://guidelines.diabetes.ca/cpg/chapter11

title: The three levels of low
advice: A reading under 3.9 is a low worth treating. Under 3.0 is a serious low that needs action right away. A low where you need someone else's help is a severe low, and it should always prompt a talk with your team.
how: Level 1: 3.0-3.9 mmol/L. Level 2: under 3.0 mmol/L (clinically significant). Level 3: a severe event with altered thinking, needing help from another person, at any number. Diabetes Canada defines a low as under 4.0 mmol/L for people on insulin. ADA says a level 2 or 3 low means the treatment plan should be re-evaluated.
why: Below about 3.0 mmol/L, brain function and the body's warning symptoms start to fail, so the risk rises sharply.
sources: International Hypoglycaemia Study Group, Diabetes Care 2017, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc16-2215
ADA Standards of Care 2026, Sec. 6, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc26-S006
Diabetes Canada CPG Ch. 14 Hypoglycemia (Yale, Paty, Senior), 2018, https://www.diabetes.ca/for-professionals/full-guidelines/chapter-14

title: Getting your low warning signs back
advice: After many years with type 1, and especially with frequent lows, the warning signs often get weaker. The encouraging part is that strictly avoiding lows for a few weeks can bring some of that awareness back.
how: ADA recommends that people with hypoglycemia unawareness, a severe low, or a pattern of unexplained lows below 3.0 raise their glycemic goals to strictly avoid hypoglycemia for at least several weeks; this partially reverses unawareness. Diabetes Canada recommends targets loosened for up to 3 months, plus CGM and education. In practice: aim a bit higher for a while, and treat at the low alert rather than waiting for symptoms. Ask your team about a structured program (for example BGAT/HypoAware-style training) and about checking your awareness with the Gold or Clarke questionnaire.
why: Each low dampens the body's adrenaline response to the next one for a day or more (hypoglycemia-associated autonomic failure), and avoiding lows lets that response recover.
sources: ADA Standards of Care 2026, Sec. 6, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc26-S006
Diabetes Canada CPG Ch. 14 Hypoglycemia, Rec. 3-4, 2018, https://www.diabetes.ca/for-professionals/full-guidelines/chapter-14
Cryer PE, Mechanisms of hypoglycemia-associated autonomic failure, NEJM 2013, https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMra1215228

title: Protect insulin from heat
advice: Insulin that's been in a hot car or in direct sun can lose strength.
how: Pen in use at room temperature for up to 28 days (check label); spare pens in the fridge; insulated cooling cases (Frio) in summer.
why: Heat degrades insulin proteins.
sources: Diabetes UK Forum, 'Insulin absorption factors', https://forum.diabetes.org.uk/boards/threads/insulin-absorption-factors.2739

title: Track the active insulin on injections
advice: Pumps track active insulin for you; on pens, you have to do it yourself. That's where a lot of stacking lows come from.
how: Log every rapid shot with the time, in a smart pen (InPen, NovoPen 6 with logging), a cap like Tempo, or a notes app. Before any correction, check what's still working from the last 3-4 hours.
why: Rapid insulin keeps working 3-5 hours, so a second shot adds to the first.
sources: Diabetes UK Forum, 'Bad BG readings' (half-correction advice), https://forum.diabetes.org.uk/boards/threads/bad-bg-readings.87199/latest
One Drop blog, 'High (and low) blood sugars are not forever' (rage bolus), https://onedrop.today/blogs/blog/rage-bolus-high-blood-sugar-overeat-low-blood-sugar-how-to-control-diabetes-emotions

title: Avoid stacking insulin
advice: Rapid insulin keeps working for about 4 hours. Taking another correction because the number hasn't come down yet adds up, and that's a classic cause of late-morning and afternoon lows. Give the first dose time to work.
