how: Before any correction, ask yourself when you last took rapid insulin. Within about 3 hours, assume a good part of it is still active and hold off or correct cautiously. Use the CGM arrow: if you're high but the arrow is flat or down within 2-3 hours of a dose, the insulin is working. Write down correction times. A smart pen or the dose memory in a pen app shows insulin on board. Ask your team for a correction rule that accounts for active insulin.
why: Overlapping doses add their effects together, so the total working insulin ends up far more than you intended.
sources: Holt RIG et al., ADA/EASD T1D Consensus, Diabetes Care 2021, https://doi.org/10.2337/dci21-0043

title: Insulin storage and expiry
advice: Insulin that's been too warm, frozen, or open too long can quietly lose strength, which shows up as highs that don't respond like they used to. Store it properly and note the date you open each pen.
how: Unopened pens or vials: in the fridge at 2-8 °C, never frozen. In use: room temperature, up to about 28 days for most rapid insulins and glargine U100; longer for some (for example degludec, glargine U300). Check the leaflet. Write the date you open it on the pen. Keep insulin out of a hot car, direct sun and the freezer side of the fridge. Discard it if it's cloudy when it should be clear, or if it has been frozen. Prime (air-shot) the pen before each injection as the leaflet describes.
why: Heat and freezing break down the insulin protein, so the same number of units does less.
sources: ADA Standards of Care 2026, Sec. 9 Pharmacologic Approaches, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc26-S009
Frid AH et al., Mayo Clin Proc 2016, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.mayocp.2016.06.010

title: Juice box at the bedside for night lows
advice: At 3 a.m. you want something you can get down half asleep without chewing. A small juice box on the nightstand does the job.
how: Keep 2-3 small (125-200 mL) juice boxes or a pouch of glucose gel within arm's reach. Some prefer half a box for a slow drop and the whole one for a fast drop. Others keep tabs but say they're hard to chew when groggy.
why: Liquid sugar empties from the stomach fastest and needs no chewing.
caveat: Juice overshoots some people; know your amount (and note it on the box).
sources: Breakthrough T1D Forum, 'Tips for night time snacks', https://forum.breakthrought1d.org/t/tips-for-night-time-snacks/74280
Breakthrough T1D Forum, '15/15 rule outdated? If so, what is better way?', https://forum.breakthrought1d.org/t/15-15-rule-outdated-if-so-what-is-better-way/75173

title: Reading Canadian nutrition labels for carbs
advice: On Canadian labels, the number to use is 'Carbohydrate' - fibre is already included in it. Many people find subtracting fibre for high-fibre foods gives a closer match.
how: Use total carbohydrate per serving, then scale to your portion. For foods with 5 g or more fibre per serving, some educators suggest subtracting the fibre; check with your team whether that suits you. Watch serving sizes - a 'serving' of bagel is often half a bagel.
why: Fibre is not digested into glucose, so very high-fibre foods raise glucose less than their total carb suggests.
sources: Diabetes Canada CPG Ch.11 Nutrition Therapy (Sievenpiper et al.), 2018, https://guidelines.diabetes.ca/cpg/chapter11
Health Canada. Canadian Nutrient File, n.d., https://food-nutrition.canada.ca/cnf-fce/

title: Late-morning lows
advice: Lows around 10 a.m. to noon usually come from breakfast insulin outpacing a light breakfast, a correction on top of breakfast, or a morning walk. If there's no breakfast insulin involved, the long-acting may be part of it too.
how: Look for: a small breakfast with a usual dose, a correction for a morning high plus the breakfast dose (stacking), activity in the morning, or a late lunch. Fix tactics: eat lunch on time, carry glucose tablets, and talk to your team about the breakfast ratio, or about the basal if the low happens even on days you skip breakfast insulin.
why: Breakfast rapid insulin peaks 1-2 hours later, and morning insulin sensitivity rises as dawn hormones fade.
sources: Holt RIG et al., ADA/EASD T1D Consensus, Diabetes Care 2021, https://doi.org/10.2337/dci21-0043

title: Late-morning lows: look at the breakfast dose
advice: Lows 2-4 hours after breakfast usually mean the breakfast shot is a little strong for what you ate, or you were busier than usual.
how: Check: was the breakfast low-carb but dosed like usual? Were you active (shopping, cleaning)? Some people add protein at breakfast, keep a 10 g snack at mid-morning, or discuss a different breakfast ratio. Morning basal (if you switched to morning dosing) can also contribute.
why: Breakfast often needs more insulin early but less later, as insulin sensitivity improves during the morning.
sources: Diabetes UK Forum, 'Late morning going high and I don't know the reason', https://forum.diabetes.org.uk/boards/threads/late-morning-going-high-and-i-don%E2%80%99t-know-the-reason.89608
Gary Scheiner, 'Think Like a Pancreas' (book, 3rd ed.), 2020 (basal testing, exercise and meal-dosing chapters)

title: Late-morning lows after coffee breakfast
advice: If coffee with creamer and milk is your main breakfast and you dose for it, a late-morning low can happen when insulin outlasts the fairly quick carbs in the drink. Looking at what's in the mug and what comes after can help pinpoint why.
how: Check the real carbs: milk is about 12 g per cup (250 mL), 18% cream about 1 g per tbsp, flavoured creamers 5-6 g per tbsp, and sugar-free sweeteners 0-1 g. If there's no food with it, adding a little protein/fibre (egg, yogurt, toast with peanut butter) may smooth the curve. Recurring 10-11 am lows are worth showing your team.
why: A liquid breakfast absorbs fast, while rapid insulin lasts 3-4 hours, so insulin can outrun the carbs by mid-morning.
sources: Health Canada. Canadian Nutrient File, n.d., https://food-nutrition.canada.ca/cnf-fce/
ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026, Section 6 Glycemic Goals and Hypoglycemia, 2026, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc26-S006

title: Lumpy injection spots cause unpredictable sugars
advice: After 30 years of injections, it's very common to have rubbery or lumpy areas under the skin. Insulin absorbs unpredictably there, causing surprise highs and lows. Ask your nurse to check your sites, and spread your injections out.
how: Feel your usual spots for thickened or rubbery skin; flat palms work better than fingertips. Rotate within each area and keep injections about 1 cm (a finger-width) apart. Use a new pen needle every time; the 4 mm needle is enough for most adults. Important: if you move from a lumpy area to healthy skin, the insulin works more strongly and you may go low. Tell your team before switching so they can plan for possibly needing less.
why: Lipohypertrophy, a fatty thickening from repeated injections in the same place, makes insulin absorption erratic and delayed, which raises variability and unexplained lows.
sources: Frid AH et al., New Insulin Delivery Recommendations, Mayo Clin Proc 2016, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.mayocp.2016.06.010
FIT Canada Forum for Injection Technique recommendations, https://www.fit4diabetes.com/

title: Sweet drinks: save them for lows
advice: Juice and regular pop raise glucose so fast that insulin can't keep up, which is exactly why they're great for lows and tricky for everyday drinking.
how: Keep juice and regular pop as low treatment, and choose water, diet pop, sparkling water, or unsweetened tea/coffee day to day. If you love juice, having it with a meal and a small portion (125 mL) helps.
why: Liquid sugars bypass chewing and slow digestion, absorbing in minutes.
sources: Diabetes Canada CPG Ch.11 Nutrition Therapy (Sievenpiper et al.), 2018, https://guidelines.diabetes.ca/cpg/chapter11
Evert AB et al. Nutrition Therapy for Adults With Diabetes or Prediabetes: A Consensus Report. Diabetes Care, 2019, https://doi.org/10.2337/dci19-0014

title: When to follow a low with a snack
advice: After your glucose is back up, a small snack can help if your next meal is more than an hour away, or if the low happened overnight. It isn't always needed.
how: Follow-up options with about 15 g carbs plus protein: 4-6 crackers with cheese, half a peanut butter sandwich, a small yogurt, an apple with nuts. Skip it if a meal is coming within the hour.
why: Fast sugar wears off quickly; slower carbs plus protein keep glucose steady while active insulin is still working.
sources: Diabetes Canada CPG Ch.14 Hypoglycemia, 2018, https://guidelines.diabetes.ca/cpg/chapter14

title: A low kit everywhere
advice: Having fast sugar within arm's reach is one of the most practical safety habits - nightstand, purse, car, coat pocket, and desk. It also cuts down on overtreating with whatever's nearby.
how: Stock tubes of Dex4 or a few small juice boxes in each spot. Check expiry dates every few months. Ask your team about glucagon (e.g., nasal glucagon) for severe lows and show a family member how to use it.
why: Rapid access shortens time spent low and reduces risk of a severe episode.
sources: Diabetes Canada CPG Ch.14 Hypoglycemia, 2018, https://guidelines.diabetes.ca/cpg/chapter14
ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026, Section 6 Glycemic Goals and Hypoglycemia, 2026, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc26-S006

title: Lower-carb meals can steady things (optional)
advice: Some people find that eating fewer carbs at a meal means smaller doses and smaller mistakes. It's an option to try, not a rule.
how: Common versions: carbs around 30 g at a meal instead of 60-80 g, more vegetables, protein and healthy fats. Adam Brown's 'eat less than 30 g at a meal' is a popular community idea.
why: Smaller carb loads mean smaller insulin doses, so errors in either cause smaller swings.
caveat: Very low-carb eating can raise the risk of lows and change how glucagon works; it is not a requirement. Talk to your dietitian.
sources: Adam Brown / diaTribe, 'Bright Spots & Landmines' (free book), 2017, https://diatribe.org/bright-spots-and-landmines

title: One low makes the next one more likely
advice: A low overnight makes it harder to notice a low the next day, so the lows tend to come in runs. After a rough night, be extra careful the following day.
how: On the day after a night-time low: check the Dexcom more often, treat at the alert rather than waiting for symptoms, eat meals on time, go easier on corrections and on hard exercise, and don't drive unless you're above 5.0 and stable.
why: A recent low blunts the hormonal and symptom response to the next one for about 24-72 hours.
sources: Cryer PE, NEJM 2013, https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMra1215228
Holt RIG et al., ADA/EASD T1D Consensus, Diabetes Care 2021, https://doi.org/10.2337/dci21-0043

title: Keep low supplies everywhere you spend time
advice: After 30 years you know lows come at bad moments. The trick is never having to go looking.
how: Stash tabs or candies in: bedside table, car door/console, every purse and jacket, desk drawer, gym bag, the TV room, and a ziplock in the bathroom. Restock on Sundays. Some people keep a 'low box' in the kitchen with pre-counted portions so the household knows what to grab.
why: Delay in treating is what turns a mild low into a severe one.
caveat: Juice and gummies degrade in hot cars; tabs travel better.
sources: Adam Brown / diaTribe, 'Bright Spots & Landmines' (free book), 2017, https://diatribe.org/bright-spots-and-landmines
Breakthrough T1D Forum, '15/15 rule outdated? If so, what is better way?', https://forum.breakthrought1d.org/t/15-15-rule-outdated-if-so-what-is-better-way/75173

title: Regular meals on a fixed basal
advice: With a once-daily long-acting insulin, your background insulin keeps working whether you eat or not. Fairly regular meals can make the day more predictable - and if lows happen when meals are late, that's useful information.
how: Try to eat roughly every 4-6 hours while awake. If you know lunch will be late, carry a 15-20 g snack (granola bar, fruit, crackers). Note on your log when lows happen with skipped or delayed meals and share it with your team.
why: Long-acting basal is meant to cover only background needs; if it's set slightly high, skipping meals unmasks it as lows.
sources: Diabetes Canada CPG Ch.11 Nutrition Therapy (Sievenpiper et al.), 2018, https://guidelines.diabetes.ca/cpg/chapter11
ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026, Section 5 Facilitating Positive Health Behaviors, 2026, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc26-S005

title: Treat lows with something pre-counted
advice: The easiest way to stop a low turning into a high is to treat with something already counted out, so you are not deciding while your brain is running on empty.
how: People keep glucose tabs (4 g each in Canada, e.g. Dex4), 200 mL juice boxes (~20-25 g), or a roll of Rockets/Smarties candies (~6-7 g a roll) and treat with a fixed amount: about 15 g for a typical low, 8-10 g for a gentle drift down from 4.5. Many say a measured item 'stops the hand going back to the pantry'.
why: Pure glucose absorbs predictably and fast; a fixed portion takes the guesswork and the hunger-driven overeating out of it.
caveat: A fast-falling low (two down arrows) or one with a lot of rapid insulin on board may need more than 15 g.
sources: Breakthrough T1D Forum, '15/15 rule outdated? If so, what is better way?', https://forum.breakthrought1d.org/t/15-15-rule-outdated-if-so-what-is-better-way/75173
diaTribe, 'Defeating the Hypoglycemia Binge', https://diatribe.org/diabetes-management/defeating-hypoglycemia-binge
Healthline, 'Rule of 15 for diabetes', https://www.healthline.com/health/diabetes/rule-of-15-diabetes

title: Hormone cycle effects
advice: Many women see higher sugars in the week before their period, then a drop and more lows once it starts. If your lows cluster at certain times of the month, that's worth tracking. Perimenopause can make it less predictable.
how: Note period days in the Dexcom or a calendar for 2-3 cycles and compare. If there's a clear pattern, ask your team about a planned temporary adjustment for those days, and be ready for lows as the period begins.
why: Progesterone in the luteal phase raises insulin resistance, and when it falls at menstruation, insulin sensitivity rises again.
sources: Brown SA et al., Fluctuations of hyperglycemia and insulin sensitivity are linked to menstrual cycle phases in women with T1D, J Diabetes Sci Technol 2015, https://doi.org/10.1177/1932296815608400

title: Did I take my long-acting? Avoid doubling
advice: A surprise low that lasts many hours can come from accidentally taking the long-acting twice. It's an easy mistake after 30 years of doing it on autopilot. A simple tracking habit prevents it.
how: Use a smart pen cap or a pen with dose memory (for example a Timesulin-style cap or InPen/NovoPen 6 memory), or tick a box on the fridge calendar. If you think you double-dosed: tell your team or call Telehealth (811 in most provinces). Set the CGM low alert higher for 24 hours, eat regularly, don't exercise hard, and make sure someone knows. If you're unsure whether you took it, don't simply take another dose; call your team for a plan.
why: An extra long-acting dose works for about 24 hours, causing a prolonged low that keeps coming back.
sources: Holt RIG et al., ADA/EASD T1D Consensus, Diabetes Care 2021, https://doi.org/10.2337/dci21-0043

title: Switch long-acting from bedtime to morning
advice: A lot of people with Lantus or Basaglar at bedtime find it peaks a little in the night. Moving it to the morning is a common, well-tolerated change.
how: People move the shot to breakfast time (often in steps over a few days) and many report fewer 1-3 a.m. lows. Do this with your team's guidance on how to bridge the switch day.
why: Glargine has a mild peak several hours after injection; dosing in the morning puts that peak in the daytime when you're awake and eating.
caveat: Some get a rise in the late evening/early night as the dose wanes; that's when splitting is considered.
sources: Diabetes UK Forum, 'Splitting Lantus dose' thread, https://forum.diabetes.org.uk/boards/threads/splitting-lantus-dose.15061
Diabetes UK Forum, 'Basal insulin at night' thread, https://forum.diabetes.org.uk/boards/threads/basal-insulin-at-night.94866/latest

title: Nachos: hard to count, easy to underestimate
advice: Nachos are one of the hardest foods to count because the chip pile is hidden under cheese. People often underestimate them, then see a long, late high from all the cheese.
how: Tortilla chips are about 1 g carb per chip, or roughly 18-20 g per 28 g (about 10-12 chips). A restaurant platter can be 80-150 g carbs for the whole thing - decide your share up front. Plate your portion instead of grazing; beans and salsa add fibre.
why: Large amounts of fried corn starch plus melted cheese cause both a sizeable carb load and delayed absorption.
sources: CalorieKing food database, n.d., https://www.calorieking.com
Bell KJ et al. Impact of Fat, Protein, and Glycemic Index on Postprandial Glucose Control in Type 1 Diabetes. Diabetes Care, 2015, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc15-0100

title: Use a fresh pen needle
advice: Reusing pen needles is common, but it dulls them, adds to lumps, and can make doses less predictable.
how: Change the needle each shot if you can; 4 mm needles are enough for most adults.
why: Dull needles damage tissue, contributing to lipohypertrophy.
sources: Review on lipohypertrophy and erratic absorption (PMC8442188), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8442188

title: There is no one right diet for T1D
advice: Major guidelines agree there's no single 'diabetes diet' - the best eating pattern is one that fits your tastes, culture, budget and life. The goal is matching insulin to what you actually like to eat, not cutting foods out.
how: Start from what you already eat (coffee, burgers, pizza, bagels) and look for one small tweak at a time rather than a whole new plan. Ask for a referral to a registered dietitian who works with T1D; in Canada this is often free through a diabetes education centre.
why: Evidence shows many eating patterns (Mediterranean, lower-carb, DASH, vegetarian) can work, so personal fit and sustainability matter more than the label.
sources: Evert AB et al. Nutrition Therapy for Adults With Diabetes or Prediabetes: A Consensus Report. Diabetes Care, 2019, https://doi.org/10.2337/dci19-0014
Diabetes Canada CPG Ch.11 Nutrition Therapy (Sievenpiper et al.), 2018, https://guidelines.diabetes.ca/cpg/chapter11
ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026, Section 5 Facilitating Positive Health Behaviors, 2026, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc26-S005

title: No good or bad foods
advice: All foods can fit with type 1 diabetes. After decades of living with it, many people feel tired of food rules - the focus is on learning how each food behaves for you, not on restriction.
how: When a meal goes high or low, treat it as information: note what you ate, timing, and the CGM curve. Pick one food you eat often and experiment with it for a week. Celebrate meals that go well.
why: Food guilt and restriction can increase stress and disordered eating risk, which itself worsens glucose management.
sources: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026, Section 5 Facilitating Positive Health Behaviors, 2026, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc26-S005
Evert AB et al. Nutrition Therapy for Adults With Diabetes or Prediabetes: A Consensus Report. Diabetes Care, 2019, https://doi.org/10.2337/dci19-0014

title: Raise the overnight Low alert so you get warned early
advice: With frequent night lows, an earlier warning buys you time to take a few grams before it becomes a real low.
how: Many people set the Low alert around 4.4-5.0 mmol/L overnight, keep Urgent Low Soon on (warns ~20 min before 3.1), and turn on Falling Fast. G7 lets you add a second, scheduled night profile in Alerts so daytime settings stay as you like them.
why: An early alert catches the drop while a small treatment is still enough.
caveat: Too many alerts lead to alarm fatigue; adjust the threshold so it's useful, not constant.
sources: Dexcom Canada FAQ, 'How could I prevent nighttime lows with earlier alerts?', https://www.dexcom.com/en-ca/faqs/g7/how-could-i-prevent-nighttime-lows-with-earlier-alerts
Dexcom FAQ, 'How can I get fewer nighttime alerts with G7?', https://www.dexcom.com/en-us/faqs/how-can-i-get-fewer-nighttime-alerts

title: Long overnight lows usually point to the long-acting
advice: When you drift low overnight and stay there for hours, well after supper's rapid insulin has worn off, it usually means your long-acting is a bit strong for the night. That's a question for your team: they may trim it or change when you take it.
how: Clue: the drop starts 4-5 hours or more after the last rapid insulin, with no exercise or alcohol that day, and repeats on several nights a week. Ask your team about trimming the long-acting, changing the time you take it, or switching to a flatter basal. Until then, set the Dexcom low alert higher overnight and consider a bedtime snack when you go to bed in the lower range.
why: Rapid insulin is mostly gone 4-5 hours after a dose, so a slow overnight fall is driven by the basal insulin.
sources: Holt RIG et al., Management of Type 1 Diabetes in Adults: ADA/EASD Consensus Report, Diabetes Care 2021, https://doi.org/10.2337/dci21-0043
ADA Standards of Care 2026, Sec. 9 Pharmacologic Approaches, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc26-S009

title: Agree with your husband on what Follow alerts mean
advice: Having your husband on Dexcom Follow can be a real comfort, especially at night. It works best when you've agreed what he should do and when.
how: Agree on thresholds: e.g., he gets notified only for lows or urgent lows overnight, not highs. Agree on the response: a text or wake you, bring juice. Agree he doesn't comment on highs unless you ask.
why: Clear agreements prevent nagging and keep the focus on safety.
sources: diaTribe, 'How to Coach Your Care-Partner on CGM Data', https://diatribe.org/lifestyle/how-coach-your-care-partner-cgm-data
TCOYD type 1 talks (diabetes 'couples therapy' session on not being the diabetes police), https://tcoyd.org/tag/type-1/

title: How a partner can help during a low
advice: During a low, you might be irritable or confused; a partner's calm help is valuable.
how: Partners: hand over the juice without questioning, avoid 'Did you take too much?', wait 15 minutes together, then talk later if needed.
why: Low blood sugar affects the brain, so arguing doesn't help.
sources: TCOYD type 1 talks (diabetes 'couples therapy' session on not being the diabetes police), https://tcoyd.org/tag/type-1/
diaTribe, 'How to Coach Your Care-Partner on CGM Data', https://diatribe.org/lifestyle/how-coach-your-care-partner-cgm-data

title: Partner Follow without nagging
advice: It's easy for a loving partner to become the 'diabetes police'. You decide how much he weighs in.
how: Some couples set Follow to only alert for urgent lows; partner asks 'Need anything?' rather than 'Why are you high?'.
why: Respecting autonomy reduces diabetes distress.
sources: diaTribe, 'How to Coach Your Care-Partner on CGM Data', https://diatribe.org/lifestyle/how-coach-your-care-partner-cgm-data
TCOYD type 1 talks (diabetes 'couples therapy' session on not being the diabetes police), https://tcoyd.org/tag/type-1/

title: Connect with others who get it
advice: Talking to others with type 1 can make things feel lighter and give you new ideas.
how: Online forums, Facebook groups, local in-person groups (e.g., Connected in Motion in Canada for adults with T1D), podcasts like Juicebox.
why: Peer support reduces isolation and offers practical tips.
caveat: Forum advice varies; check dose changes with your team.
sources: NDSS (Australia), 'Diabetes distress and burnout', https://www.ndss.com.au/looking-after-your-mind/when-diabetes-makes-it-tough/diabetes-distress-and-burnout/

Juicebox Podcast (Scott Benner), 'Type 1 Diabetes Pro Tips' series: Pre Bolus, Bump and Nudge (#34, #44), Setting Basal Insulin (#37), Fat and Protein (#39), https://podbay.fm/p/type-1-diabetes-pro-tips

title: Pho and noodle soups
advice: Noodle soups are tricky because the noodles hide under the broth. A large pho bowl often has more carbs than people think.
how: A regular bowl of pho typically has 40-60 g carbs from noodles; large 70-90 g. Hoisin sauce adds ~5 g per tbsp. Options: order a small, ask for extra veg/sprouts, or leave some noodles. Ramen is similar or higher.
why: Rice noodles are refined starch that digests quickly, especially in hot broth.
sources: CalorieKing food database, n.d., https://www.calorieking.com

title: How guidelines phrase dose changes
advice: Ray names the lever ('your long-acting may be strong overnight', 'the breakfast ratio may be a bit strong') and steers the actual number change to her diabetes team, the way guidelines describe adjustments as shared decisions.
how: Guidelines frame these as shared decision-making: 're-evaluate the treatment plan' after level 2 or 3 lows (ADA); 'raise glycemic goals' to restore awareness; 'consider basal reduction' after evening exercise (consensus). Good phrasings: 'worth asking your team about trimming your long-acting', 'ask whether a different long-acting would suit you', 'ask for a bedtime correction rule'. Never state units or percentages for her.
why: Safe insulin adjustment depends on the full clinical picture, and the guidelines place dose decisions with the care team or a trained, structured-education patient.
sources: ADA Standards of Care 2026, Sec. 6, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc26-S006
Holt RIG et al., ADA/EASD T1D Consensus, Diabetes Care 2021, https://doi.org/10.2337/dci21-0043

title: The pizza effect
advice: Pizza is famous among people with T1D for causing a low or flat line in the first couple of hours, then a stubborn high late in the evening or overnight. You're not doing anything wrong - it's one of the trickiest foods there is.
how: Count the crust carefully (a large slice can be 30-40 g carbs; thick or stuffed crust more). Add a salad first to slow things and help fullness. Having pizza earlier in the evening rather than late means the delayed rise happens while you're awake to see it.
why: Cheese and meat fat delay gastric emptying of the crust's starch, shifting the glucose rise 3-6 hours later than usual.
sources: Bell KJ et al. Impact of Fat, Protein, and Glycemic Index on Postprandial Glucose Control in Type 1 Diabetes. Diabetes Care, 2015, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc15-0100
Paterson M et al. The Role of Dietary Protein and Fat in Glycaemic Control in Type 1 Diabetes. Curr Diab Rep, 2015, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4512569

title: Pizza, pasta and Chinese food: split the shot
advice: Big, fatty meals digest slowly. One shot up front can cause a low early and a high hours later. Splitting the dose on injections is a common workaround.
how: MDI version of an 'extended bolus': part of the dose at the start of the meal and the rest 1-2 hours later (community splits range from 50/50 to 60/40, with any correction in the first shot). Set a phone reminder for the second shot.
why: Fat and protein slow stomach emptying, delaying the carb rise by hours.
caveat: Split ratios are personal; test on a weekend with your team's input. Forgetting the second shot means a high.
sources: diaTribe, 'Pizza and Blood Sugar Control: (Not Quite) Easy as Pie', https://diatribe.org/diet-and-nutrition/pizza-and-blood-sugar-control-not-quite-easy-pie
Diabetes UK Forum, 'Double injecting for pasta', https://forum.diabetes.org.uk/boards/threads/double-injecting-for-pasta.20889/latest
Diabetes UK Forum, 'Fat, protein and carbs question (oh and booze)', https://forum.diabetes.org.uk/boards/threads/fat-protein-and-carbs-question-oh-and-booze.103293
Beyond Type 1, 'Bolus for pizza tips', https://beyondtype1.org/bolus-for-pizza-tips/

title: The plate method when you can't count
advice: When counting carbs precisely isn't practical, the plate method gives a consistent meal shape: half vegetables, a quarter protein, a quarter starch. Consistency makes your insulin estimate more predictable.
how: Use a standard 9-inch plate: 1/2 non-starchy veg, 1/4 protein, 1/4 grains/starch, plus a fruit and milk if you like. For a quarter-plate starch, many people find it's roughly 30-45 g carbs - check a few times with a measuring cup to calibrate.
why: Keeping the carb portion steady and pairing it with fibre and protein reduces both carb-estimate error and peak height.
sources: Diabetes Canada. Meal planning / Just the Basics plate method, n.d., https://diabetes.ca/nutrition---fitness/meal-planning
Diabetes Canada CPG Ch.11 Nutrition Therapy (Sievenpiper et al.), 2018, https://guidelines.diabetes.ca/cpg/chapter11

title: Why you might go low after meals
advice: A low 1 to 3 hours after a meal usually means the insulin for that meal was more than you needed. Common reasons are a dose that's too strong for that meal, over-counted carbs, pre-bolusing too long, or being active after eating. Look at which meal it happens after.
how: Check, for the meal in question: was the carb count high? Was the pre-bolus long? Were you active after eating? Was there a correction on top? Was it a high-fat meal (insulin peaks before the food is absorbed)? If it's the same meal on 3 or more days, your team may adjust the insulin-to-carb ratio for that meal. Your body may also need less insulin at breakfast than at supper, or the other way round.
why: The mealtime dose peaks 1-2 hours after injection, so too much of it shows up as a low in that window.
sources: Holt RIG et al., ADA/EASD T1D Consensus, Diabetes Care 2021, https://doi.org/10.2337/dci21-0043
Diabetes Canada CPG Ch. 12 Glycemic Management in Adults with T1D, 2018, https://www.diabetes.ca/for-professionals/full-guidelines/chapter-12

title: What counts as a good after-meal number
advice: Some rise after eating is normal. The goal is to stay under 10 at the peak and be back near your starting point by 3 to 4 hours, without dropping low.
how: Diabetes Canada targets: before meals 4.0-7.0 mmol/L; 2 hours after meals 5.0-10.0 mmol/L (5.0-8.0 if the A1C target isn't being met). ADA: peak after meals under 10.0 mmol/L. For you, avoiding lows comes first, so a few post-meal readings slightly above 10 are an acceptable trade.
why: Post-meal highs add to A1C and variability, but chasing them aggressively causes lows.
sources: Diabetes Canada CPG Ch. 8 Targets for Glycemic Control, 2018, https://www.diabetes.ca/for-professionals/full-guidelines/chapter-8
ADA Standards of Care 2026, Sec. 6, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc26-S006

title: Poutine
advice: Poutine is a Canadian classic that combines lots of fries, gravy and cheese - big carbs and big fat, so expect a later rise. You can absolutely enjoy it with some planning.
how: A regular poutine is often 60-90 g carbs; large can be 100 g or more. Check chain nutrition info (e.g., New York Fries, Smoke's, A&W). A smaller size, sharing, or adding a side salad helps. Watch your CGM 3-5 hours later to learn your pattern.
why: Fried potato starch digests fairly quickly, but the cheese and gravy fat slow and extend the rise.
sources: CalorieKing food database, n.d., https://www.calorieking.com
Bell KJ et al. Impact of Fat, Protein, and Glycemic Index on Postprandial Glucose Control in Type 1 Diabetes. Diabetes Care, 2015, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc15-0100

title: Pre-bolus 15-20 minutes when in range
advice: If you're in range and steady, taking your mealtime insulin about 15 to 20 minutes before you eat can flatten the after-meal spike a lot. But if you're on the low side or dropping, bolus right as you start eating instead.
how: In range and flat: inject 15-20 minutes before eating. High: a longer wait helps. Below about 5 or falling: inject at the start of the meal, or even right after it. If you're unsure you'll finish the meal (for example eating out, or with a poor appetite), inject right after eating. Ultra-rapid insulins (Fiasp, Lyumjev) go in at the start of the meal.
why: Rapid-acting analogues take about 15 minutes to start working and peak at 1-2 hours, while carbs raise glucose within 15-30 minutes, so giving the insulin early lines it up with the food.
sources: Slattery D, Amiel SA, Choudhary P, Optimal prandial timing of bolus insulin in diabetes management: a review, Diabet Med 2018, https://doi.org/10.1111/dme.13525
Holt RIG et al., ADA/EASD T1D Consensus, Diabetes Care 2021, https://doi.org/10.2337/dci21-0043

title: Head off a low early with a small snack
advice: With a CGM you don't have to wait until you're below 4. If the alert goes off and the arrow is pointing down, a small snack of 10 to 15 grams can stop the low before it starts.
how: At about 4.4-5.0 mmol/L: with a flat arrow, about 10 g of carbs; with a slight down arrow, about 15 g; with a steep down arrow, treat as a low (15-20 g) and re-check in 15 minutes. These amounts are adapted from the EASD/ISPAD overnight and exercise tables; personalise them with your team.
why: Treating on the trend catches the fall about 15-20 minutes earlier, which avoids the deep lows that cause rebounds and loss of awareness.
sources: Moser O et al., EASD/ISPAD position statement, Diabetologia 2020, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00125-020-05263-9

title: Protein on its own rarely needs a carb count
advice: Small protein snacks - a cheese string, an egg, a handful of nuts - usually have little effect on glucose. Large protein-heavy meals (big steak) are different and can cause a slow rise hours later.
how: Use low-carb protein snacks when you're hungry but don't want to dose. For big protein meals, check your CGM 3-5 hours later to learn your own pattern.
why: In T1D, protein above roughly 75 g in a meal can raise glucose later via gluconeogenesis, but small amounts have little effect.
sources: Paterson M et al. The Role of Dietary Protein and Fat in Glycaemic Control in Type 1 Diabetes. Curr Diab Rep, 2015, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4512569

Smart CE et al. Both Dietary Protein and Fat Increase Postprandial Glucose Excursions in Children With Type 1 Diabetes, and the Effect Is Additive. Diabetes Care, 2013, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc13-0195
ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines 2022: Nutritional management in children and adolescents with diabetes (Annan et al.), 2022, https://www.ispad.org/page/ISPADGuidelines2022

title: Big protein meals can cause a slow, late rise
advice: A big steak or a large protein-heavy meal can push you up slowly, 3-5 hours later.
how: Watch the G7 for a delayed rise after big protein meals. Some people include part of the protein in their dose planning or add a later small dose (agree with your team).
why: Some protein is converted to glucose slowly in the liver.
sources: Diabetes UK Forum, 'Fat, protein and carbs question (oh and booze)', https://forum.diabetes.org.uk/boards/threads/fat-protein-and-carbs-question-oh-and-booze.103293

Juicebox Podcast (Scott Benner), 'Type 1 Diabetes Pro Tips' series: Pre Bolus, Bump and Nudge (#34, #44), Setting Basal Insulin (#37), Fat and Protein (#39), https://podbay.fm/p/type-1-diabetes-pro-tips

title: Eat the vegetables and protein first, starch last
advice: A simple trick: start the meal with the salad and the meat, and leave the bread, rice or potatoes for the second half.
how: Order: vegetables, then protein/fat, then carbs. Many people find it softens the spike without changing what they eat.
why: Fibre, protein and fat slow how quickly the stomach releases carbs.
caveat: Mostly studied in type 2; slowing carbs can mismatch a pre-bolus and cause an early low, so you may need less pre-bolus time.
sources: Adam Brown / diaTribe, 'Bright Spots & Landmines' (free book), 2017, https://diatribe.org/bright-spots-and-landmines

title: Recognise the 'rage bolus' and give yourself a rule
advice: Everyone with type 1 knows the frustrated big correction after a stubborn high. Having a rule decided in a calm moment helps more than willpower.
how: Community rules of thumb: no correction within 3-4 hours of the last rapid shot unless checked with your active-insulin math; write down the time of every correction; if you're angry, walk for 10 minutes first and re-look.
why: Rapid insulin keeps working for 3-5 hours; stacking several shots lands all at once and causes a hard low.
sources: One Drop blog, 'High (and low) blood sugars are not forever' (rage bolus), https://onedrop.today/blogs/blog/rage-bolus-high-blood-sugar-overeat-low-blood-sugar-how-to-control-diabetes-emotions
Research article on post-hypoglycemic hyperglycemia and 'rage bolus' (PMC9294577), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9294577
Diabetes UK Forum, 'Bad BG readings' (half-correction advice), https://forum.diabetes.org.uk/boards/threads/bad-bg-readings.87199/latest

title: Don't chase the rebound high after a low
advice: After a low, you'll often bounce high. That's partly the liver's emergency sugar dump and partly the extra treatment. Going in hard with insulin is how the rollercoaster keeps going.
how: Wait at least 2 hours after a low before correcting, and when you do, many people use a smaller correction than usual. Ask your team for a 'post-low' correction rule.
why: Counter-regulatory hormones (glucagon, adrenaline) raise glucose and cause temporary insulin resistance after a low.
caveat: Ketones or a high that keeps climbing for hours needs a proper correction.
sources: Research article on post-hypoglycemic hyperglycemia and 'rage bolus' (PMC9294577), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9294577
Diabetes UK Forum, 'Bad BG readings' (half-correction advice), https://forum.diabetes.org.uk/boards/threads/bad-bg-readings.87199/latest
diaTribe, 'Defeating the Hypoglycemia Binge', https://diatribe.org/diabetes-management/defeating-hypoglycemia-binge

title: Rebound highs after a low: don't chase them
advice: A high that follows a low is usually from the extra food plus your body's own emergency hormones. Correcting it hard tends to start the roller-coaster again. A gentle approach evens things out.
how: Prevent it: treat lows with measured fast sugar, not by eating until you feel better. If you rebound: wait 2-3 hours before correcting (the rise often settles on its own), then correct cautiously, accounting for insulin on board. Rebounds are a big driver of a high CV.
why: Counter-regulatory hormones (glucagon, adrenaline, cortisol) released during a low raise glucose and cause temporary insulin resistance for several hours.
sources: Diabetes Canada CPG Ch. 14 Hypoglycemia, 2018, https://www.diabetes.ca/for-professionals/full-guidelines/chapter-14
Battelino T et al., International Consensus on Time in Range, Diabetes Care 2019, https://doi.org/10.2337/dci19-0028

title: Repeated lows below 3.0 mean the plan needs changing
advice: If you're dipping below 3.0 several times a week, the insulin plan needs adjusting. It isn't something to put up with or fix with more snacks. That's worth a call to your diabetes team now rather than at your next routine visit.
how: ADA: ask about hypoglycemia at every visit, and re-evaluate the treatment plan after any level 2 or level 3 low or a pattern of them. Bring your Dexcom Clarity AGP (14 days) to the call and point out the times of day the lows cluster. Write down any patterns you notice: exercise, alcohol, late corrections, missed meals.
why: When lows keep happening at the same time of day, insulin at that time is usually greater than what the body needs, and food alone can't fix that safely.
sources: ADA Standards of Care 2026, Sec. 6, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc26-S006
Diabetes Canada CPG Ch. 14 Hypoglycemia, Rec. 1-2, 2018, https://www.diabetes.ca/for-professionals/full-guidelines/chapter-14

title: Restaurant meals: count, then watch
advice: Restaurant portions and hidden sugars often fool even experienced carb counters. Plan to check and adjust rather than nail it the first time.
how: Use the chain's nutrition info (most Canadian chains post it), apps like Calorie King, or photo-estimate; then check the G7 at 2 and 4 hours. Many keep a note of 'what worked' for regular spots.
why: Sauces, breading and sugar in restaurant food add carbs that aren't obvious.
sources: Adam Brown / diaTribe, 'Bright Spots & Landmines' (free book), 2017, https://diatribe.org/bright-spots-and-landmines
diaTribe, 'Pizza and Blood Sugar Control: (Not Quite) Easy as Pie', https://diatribe.org/diet-and-nutrition/pizza-and-blood-sugar-control-not-quite-easy-pie

title: Eating out and takeout strategies
advice: Restaurant portions are big, and food is often richer than at home. A few habits make eating out far more predictable without taking the fun out of it.
how: Look up the menu's nutrition info before you go (most Canadian chains post it). Use an app like CalorieKing, Carb Manager or MyFitnessPal for estimates. Compare the plate to your hand or known portions (a fist ~ 1 cup). Box half at the start. Note your guess and CGM result so next time you can adjust.
why: Larger portions and hidden fats/sugars increase both carb-estimate error and delayed absorption.
sources: CalorieKing food database, n.d., https://www.calorieking.com
Evert AB et al. Nutrition Therapy for Adults With Diabetes or Prediabetes: A Consensus Report. Diabetes Care, 2019, https://doi.org/10.2337/dci19-0014

title: Look at your week, not just today
advice: A quick weekly look at the patterns tells you more than stressing over every reading.
how: Use the Clarity app's overlay or weekly report: when do lows cluster? Focus on one time of day at a time. Celebrate what's working.
why: Patterns show what's systematic; single readings are noise.
sources: Adam Brown / diaTribe, 'Bright Spots & Landmines' (free book), 2017, https://diatribe.org/bright-spots-and-landmines
Dr. Stephen Ponder, Sugar Surfing presentation slides, https://abcd10.redhot.circle-interactive.co.uk/sites/default/files/resources/IPN17%20PONDER.pdf

title: Rotate injection sites and check for lumps
advice: After 30 years of injections, lumpy spots are very common. Insulin from them absorbs unpredictably, causing random highs and lows.
how: Feel for rubbery or thickened areas (often around the belly button or favourite spots). Use a rotation pattern (e.g. clockwise around the belly, 2-3 cm apart). Moving to fresh skin can make insulin work much stronger, so watch for lows when changing.
why: Repeated injections at one spot cause lipohypertrophy, which slows and scatters absorption.
caveat: When you switch from a lumpy area to fresh tissue, the same dose may act stronger.
sources: IDF Diabetes Voice, 'Lipohypertrophy causes unexplained highs and lows', https://diabetesvoice.org/en/caring-for-diabetes/lipohypertrophy-causes-unexplained-highs-and-lows/
Review on lipohypertrophy and erratic absorption (PMC8442188), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8442188

title: Treating a low: the 15-15 approach
advice: For a low under 4.0 mmol/L, Diabetes Canada recommends 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate, then re-check in 15 minutes and repeat if still under 4.0. Glucose tablets are the gold standard because they work fastest and are easy to measure.
how: Take 15 g fast sugar, wait 15 minutes, re-check (CGM may lag - confirm with a fingerstick if unsure). Repeat if still below 4.0. If your next meal is more than an hour away, follow up with a snack containing about 15 g carb plus protein.
why: Pure glucose is absorbed directly without digestion; 15 g typically raises glucose about 2.1 mmol/L within 20 minutes.
sources: Diabetes Canada CPG Ch.14 Hypoglycemia, 2018, https://guidelines.diabetes.ca/cpg/chapter14
ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026, Section 6 Glycemic Goals and Hypoglycemia, 2026, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc26-S006

title: Repeat a 'known' breakfast
advice: Having a couple of go-to breakfasts that you know how to dose makes mornings far more predictable.
how: Pick 2-3 breakfasts (e.g. eggs and one slice of toast; Greek yogurt with berries and nuts) and dose them the same way each time. Adam Brown calls these 'Bright Spots': things that already work, repeated.
why: Fewer unknowns means fewer dosing errors and less variability.
sources: Adam Brown / diaTribe, 'Bright Spots & Landmines' (free book), 2017, https://diatribe.org/bright-spots-and-landmines

title: Some long-acting insulins cause fewer night lows
advice: If overnight lows keep happening even after adjustments, it's reasonable to ask your team whether a different long-acting would suit you better. The newer, flatter ones (degludec/Tresiba or glargine U300/Toujeo) are linked to fewer night-time lows.
how: Ask: 'Would a switch to degludec or glargine U300 make sense for my overnight lows?' ADA recommends long-acting analogues to reduce hypoglycemia risk. In the SWITCH 1 trial in T1D, degludec reduced nocturnal symptomatic hypoglycemia compared with glargine U100. Any switch is managed by your team, including the dose conversion.
why: Longer-acting, peakless basal insulins release more evenly over 24 hours, which means less of a night-time peak and less day-to-day variation.
sources: Lane W et al., SWITCH 1, JAMA 2017, https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2017.7115
ADA Standards of Care 2026, Sec. 9, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc26-S009

title: Pick a sensor spot that fits how you sleep
advice: The best spot is the one you don't lie on.
how: Side-sleepers: back of the arm on the non-sleeping side, or upper buttock. People also rest the sensor arm on the other arm.
why: Avoiding pressure means fewer false alarms.
sources: Diabetes UK Forum, 'Compression lows on Dexcom G7 vs Libre 3', https://forum.diabetes.org.uk/boards/threads/compression-lows-on-dexcom-g7-vs-libre-3.118389
T1D Exchange, 'What We Learned from the Online Community in August' (compression-low, alcohol-wipe and zero-sugar polls), 2022, https://t1dexchange.org/articles/top-questions-of-the-day-august-2022

title: Eating on sick days
advice: When you're sick, it's important to keep getting carbs and fluids even if you don't feel like eating, because you'll still need insulin. Your team's sick-day plan should guide dose changes.
how: If you can't eat normally, aim for about 15 g carbs every hour or so from easy foods: 1/2 cup regular jello, 125 mL juice, a popsicle, 6 soda crackers, 1 cup broth soup with noodles. Sip fluids often. Check ketones if glucose is above ~14 mmol/L, and call your team if you can't keep fluids down.
why: Illness raises stress hormones and insulin needs, while poor intake risks lows and ketones.
sources: Diabetes Canada CPG Appendix 8: Sick-Day Medication List / Ch.15 Hyperglycemic emergencies, 2018, https://guidelines.diabetes.ca/cpg/chapter15
ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines 2022: Nutritional management in children and adolescents with diabetes (Annan et al.), 2022, https://www.ispad.org/page/ISPADGuidelines2022

title: Sick days: keep the basal, check more
advice: Even if you can't eat much, keep taking your long-acting insulin and check more often. Illness usually raises sugar.
how: Check every 2-4 hours, drink fluids, have regular ginger ale or juice if you can't eat, check ketones if over 14. Call your team for dose advice.
why: Illness hormones increase insulin resistance; stopping basal risks DKA.
caveat: Vomiting with high ketones means urgent care.
sources: Diabetes Canada, 'Sick day medication list / sick-day management' (Clinical Practice Guidelines patient resources), https://www.diabetes.ca

title: Sick days: never stop the long-acting
advice: When you're sick, keep taking your long-acting even if you're not eating. Illness usually pushes sugars up. Check more often and check for ketones if you're high.
how: Check glucose every 2-4 hours. Drink plenty of sugar-free fluids, and switch to sugary fluids if you can't eat. Check blood ketones when glucose is above about 14 mmol/L or you're vomiting: 0.6-1.4 means take action per your sick-day plan; 1.5-2.9 means call your team; 3.0 or higher, or vomiting you can't stop, means go to emergency. If vomiting means you can't keep food down, you may also run low, so ask your team for a written sick-day plan that covers both.
why: Stress hormones from illness raise glucose and ketone production, and stopping basal insulin can lead to DKA within hours.
sources: Diabetes Canada CPG Ch. 15 Hyperglycemic Emergencies in Adults, 2018, https://www.diabetes.ca/for-professionals/full-guidelines/chapter-15
ADA Standards of Care 2026, Sec. 6 (Hyperglycemic Crises), https://doi.org/10.2337/dc26-S006

title: Skipping meals and lows
advice: If you get low when you skip a meal or eat late, that can be a sign your long-acting dose is doing more than background work. It's worth flagging rather than just eating to keep up with it.
how: As an experiment your team may suggest, keep a 'basal check' log: skip or delay a meal on a quiet day, don't take correction insulin, and note glucose every hour. Bring the results to your next appointment - only your team should adjust doses.
why: Basal insulin set correctly keeps glucose flat without food; a steady drop during fasting suggests it's too strong.
sources: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026, Section 6 Glycemic Goals and Hypoglycemia, 2026, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc26-S006
ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines 2022: Nutritional management in children and adolescents with diabetes (Annan et al.), 2022, https://www.ispad.org/page/ISPADGuidelines2022

title: Regular sleep and meal times help
advice: Your long-acting works the same every day, so it works best when your meals and sleep are fairly regular too. A late or skipped supper is a common setup for an overnight low.
how: Keep supper within a roughly consistent window. If you skip a meal, skip its rapid insulin too, but never the long-acting. Late night eating with a bolus puts that insulin's peak in the middle of the night. Short sleep raises insulin resistance the next day.
why: A fixed basal dose assumes a predictable daily rhythm, and big swings in routine create mismatches.
sources: ADA Standards of Care 2026, Sec. 5, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc26-S005
Holt RIG et al., ADA/EASD T1D Consensus, Diabetes Care 2021, https://doi.org/10.2337/dci21-0043

title: Change basal in small steps and wait
advice: When basal does need changing, small steps and patience beat big swings.
how: Community habit: change by a small amount, then wait 3 days (longer with Tresiba) before judging. Some people use half-unit pens (e.g. NovoPen Echo, HumaPen Luxura HD) because one whole unit flips nights from high to low.
why: Long-acting insulin takes a few days to reach a new steady state.
caveat: Agree the step size with your team.
sources: Diabetes UK Forum, 'Bedtime snacks for type 1 diabetic', https://forum.diabetes.org.uk/boards/threads/bedtime-snacks-for-type-1-diabetic.114875
Breakthrough T1D Forum, 'Tips for night time snacks', https://forum.breakthrought1d.org/t/tips-for-night-time-snacks/74280
Diabetes UK Forum, 'Splitting Lantus dose' thread, https://forum.diabetes.org.uk/boards/threads/splitting-lantus-dose.15061

title: Small nudges instead of big corrections
advice: Small, early adjustments ('nudges') keep you smoother than waiting for a big high or low and fixing it with a big move.
how: Taking a few grams of carbs when you start to drift down, or a small correction early in a rise, instead of a large correction later. Juicebox calls this 'bump and nudge'.
why: Small early changes act on a smaller problem.
caveat: Needs careful tracking of insulin on board to avoid stacking.
sources: Juicebox Podcast (Scott Benner), 'Type 1 Diabetes Pro Tips' series: Pre Bolus, Bump and Nudge (#34, #44), Setting Basal Insulin (#37), Fat and Protein (#39), https://podbay.fm/p/type-1-diabetes-pro-tips
Dr. Stephen Ponder, Sugar Surfing presentation slides, https://abcd10.redhot.circle-interactive.co.uk/sites/default/files/resources/IPN17%20PONDER.pdf

title: Smaller carbs for slow drifts
advice: Not every low needs the full 15 g. If you're drifting gently and there's not much mealtime insulin left working, a little nudge often does it without the bounce.
how: Experienced folks scale to the trend: one 4 g tab or 2-4 fruit gummies for a slow slide around 4.0-4.5, the full 15 g for a straight-down arrow, more if a meal bolus was in the last two hours. Some find 15 g raises them ~3 mmol/L, so they halve it.
why: 1 g of glucose raises an adult roughly 0.2-0.3 mmol/L, so 15 g can easily overshoot a mild low.
caveat: Below 3.0 or with symptoms of confusion, treat fully and don't experiment.
sources: Breakthrough T1D Forum, '15/15 rule outdated? If so, what is better way?', https://forum.breakthrought1d.org/t/15-15-rule-outdated-if-so-what-is-better-way/75173
Healthline, 'Rule of 15 for diabetes', https://www.healthline.com/health/diabetes/rule-of-15-diabetes

title: When a nightly snack is hiding a dose issue
advice: If you feel you *need* a snack every night to avoid going low, that's often a sign your long-acting insulin or supper dose may be set a little strong. Eating to cover insulin isn't a long-term fix - it's worth a conversation.
how: Keep a week of notes: bedtime glucose, snack or not, overnight lowest number and time. Bring CGM overnight reports to your team. Overnight lows at the same time most nights is a pattern they'll want to see.
why: Basal insulin should keep glucose steady overnight without food; a consistent need for carbs suggests too much insulin is active.
sources: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026, Section 6 Glycemic Goals and Hypoglycemia, 2026, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc26-S006
ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines 2022: Nutritional management in children and adolescents with diabetes (Annan et al.), 2022, https://www.ispad.org/page/ISPADGuidelines2022

title: Common snack carb counts
advice: Snacks between meals can quietly add up and push glucose higher. Knowing a few numbers makes it easy to decide whether a snack needs insulin.
how: Approx: small bag chips (40 g) ~20-22 g carbs; granola bar 15-25 g; 3 cups air-popped popcorn ~18 g; medium apple ~20-25 g; banana ~25-30 g; 2 cookies 15-20 g. Under ~10-15 g, some people don't dose - ask your team about your own threshold.
why: Unmatched carbs from snacks raise glucose, while very small snacks may be covered by background insulin.
sources: Health Canada. Canadian Nutrient File, n.d., https://food-nutrition.canada.ca/cnf-fce/
CalorieKing food database, n.d., https://www.calorieking.com

title: Splitting the long-acting into two shots
advice: If one shot a day leaves you low at night and high at other times, splitting it lets you give less overnight and more in the day.
how: Common starting point from community reports: two shots about 12 hours apart, often a 50:50 split, then adjusted from CGM patterns (some settle around 60:40 with the smaller part at night). Levemir is the insulin most often split; some split Lantus/Basaglar too.
why: Two smaller doses give a flatter profile and let you shape day vs night separately.
caveat: Mixed results: some find split Lantus doses too small to last well. Do it with your diabetes team, and expect 2-3 days to settle.
sources: Diabetes UK Forum, 'Splitting Lantus dose' thread, https://forum.diabetes.org.uk/boards/threads/splitting-lantus-dose.15061
Diabetes UK Forum, 'Basal insulin at night' thread, https://forum.diabetes.org.uk/boards/threads/basal-insulin-at-night.94866/latest

title: Split or extended dosing for rich meals - ask your team
advice: Research suggests high-fat, high-protein meals need more insulin overall and that some of it works better later. On injections, some people split their meal dose into two parts - but the split and amounts are something to work out with your diabetes team.
how: Ask your team about: (1) giving part of the meal dose at the start and part 1-2 hours later for rich meals, (2) whether that applies to your usual pizza/burger/nachos meals. Bring CGM traces showing an early low then late high - that's exactly the data they need.
why: Splitting the dose lines up insulin action with the delayed fat-protein glucose rise, reducing the early low and late high.
sources: Bell KJ et al. Impact of Fat, Protein, and Glycemic Index on Postprandial Glucose Control in Type 1 Diabetes. Diabetes Care, 2015, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc15-0100

Pankowska E et al. Application of novel dual wave meal bolus (fat-protein units) in children with T1D. Pediatr Diabetes, 2009, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=Pankowska+dual+wave+bolus+fat+protein+units
ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines 2022: Nutritional management in children and adolescents with diabetes (Annan et al.), 2022, https://www.ispad.org/page/ISPADGuidelines2022

title: Stress can push you up
advice: Stress, anger or a big event can push sugar up for hours.
how: Notice patterns; some people do a short walk or breathing exercise; avoid rage bolusing.
why: Stress hormones release glucose and reduce insulin sensitivity.
sources: One Drop blog, 'High (and low) blood sugars are not forever' (rage bolus), https://onedrop.today/blogs/blog/rage-bolus-high-blood-sugar-overeat-low-blood-sugar-how-to-control-diabetes-emotions
Adam Brown / diaTribe, 'Bright Spots & Landmines' (free book), 2017, https://diatribe.org/bright-spots-and-landmines

title: Stress pushes sugars up
advice: Stress, pain and poor sleep can push your sugar up without any food. Correcting these highs aggressively can lead to a low once the stress settles.
how: Correct stress highs cautiously and watch for a later drop. Short walks or breathing exercises help some people. If stress is ongoing, mention it to your team; a persistent pattern is something to adjust for, but a single stressful day isn't.
why: Cortisol and adrenaline raise liver glucose output and cause temporary insulin resistance.
sources: ADA Standards of Care 2026, Sec. 5 Facilitating Positive Health Behaviors, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc26-S005

title: A structured T1D refresher course
advice: Even after 30 years, a structured refresher program can make a real difference to lows. These courses teach you to adjust your own insulin safely, with a team behind you.
how: Holt 2021 and Diabetes Canada recommend structured education (DAFNE-style) for all adults with T1D, and hypoglycemia-focused training (for example BGAT, HypoAware) for those with frequent lows or reduced awareness. Ask your diabetes education centre what's offered in your province.
why: Structured education programs reduce severe hypoglycemia and improve awareness in trials.
sources: Holt RIG et al., ADA/EASD T1D Consensus, Diabetes Care 2021, https://doi.org/10.2337/dci21-0043
Diabetes Canada CPG Ch. 14 Hypoglycemia, Rec. 3.2, 3.5, 2018, https://www.diabetes.ca/for-professionals/full-guidelines/chapter-14

title: Sushi rice counts
advice: Sushi looks light, but the rice is seasoned with sugar and packed tight, so carbs add up fast. Many people underestimate sushi meals.
how: Rough guide: one maki piece ~4-6 g carbs (a 6-8 piece roll ~25-40 g; tempura or specialty rolls more), one nigiri ~6-8 g. Sashimi, miso soup, edamame and seaweed salad are lower-carb sides. Count pieces as you go.
why: Sushi rice is a short-grain, sweetened high-GI rice that raises glucose quickly.
sources: CalorieKing food database, n.d., https://www.calorieking.com
University of Sydney Glycemic Index database, n.d., https://glycemicindex.com

title: Tim Hortons carb estimates
advice: Tim's is easy to dose for because full nutrition info is online - you don't have to guess. Some items are surprisingly high in carbs, especially muffins and bagels.
how: Use the Tim Hortons nutrition calculator. Ballpark: plain bagel ~55 g carbs, muffin 50-65 g, donut 25-40 g, 1 Timbit 6-9 g, English muffin breakfast sandwich ~30 g, chili ~20-25 g. A breakfast sandwich or chili are lower-carb options.
why: Published values let you match insulin to carbs accurately instead of estimating.
sources: Tim Hortons Canada. Nutrition & Allergens, n.d., https://www.timhortons.ca/nutrition-and-allergens

title: Updated CGM metric definitions (2023)
advice: The newer international statement keeps the same targets and adds that CGM numbers should sit alongside A1C. Time below range is singled out as a key safety result.
how: The 2023 consensus on CGM metrics confirms the 3.9-10.0 range, 14 or more days of data, and 70% sensor wear, and defines a hypoglycemia 'event' as 15 minutes or more below 3.9 (level 1) or below 3.0 (level 2), ending after 15 minutes back above 3.9. Use event counts and their time of day when talking with your team.
why: Counting low events by time of day shows clinicians exactly which insulin, at which time, to look at.
sources: Battelino T et al., Continuous glucose monitoring and metrics for clinical trials: an international consensus statement, Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2023, https://doi.org/10.1016/S2213-8587(22)00319-9

title: Treating a low: the 15 g rule
advice: For an ordinary low, take 15 g of fast sugar, wait 15 minutes, and check again. If you're under 3.0 or feel quite unwell, start with 20 g.
how: Below 4.0 mmol/L and awake: take 15 g of glucose or sucrose; use 20 g if you're below 3.0 or the low feels severe. Re-check after 15 minutes and take another 15 g if you're still below 4.0. Diabetes Canada prefers glucose or sucrose tablets or a solution over juice or gels. ADA says 15-20 g of glucose is the preferred treatment, and its 2026 update adds a recommendation that first-aid kits carry oral glucose. 15 g of glucose raises glucose by about 2.1 mmol/L within 20 minutes.
why: Pure glucose is absorbed quickly and predictably, so the amount you take matches the rise you get.
sources: Diabetes Canada CPG Ch. 14 Hypoglycemia, Rec. 5-6, 2018, https://www.diabetes.ca/for-professionals/full-guidelines/chapter-14
ADA Standards of Care 2026, Sec. 6, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc26-S006

title: What 15 g looks like in Canada
advice: Keep pre-measured fast sugar wherever you might go low: by the bed, in your bag, and in the car. Then you're not guessing in the middle of the night.
how: Each of these is about 15 g: 4 Dex4 tablets (4 g each); 5 Dextrosol tablets (3 g each); 15 mL (3 tsp, or 3 packets) of table sugar dissolved in water; 175 mL (3/4 cup) of juice or regular pop; 15 mL (1 tbsp) of honey; 6 Life Savers. Avoid chocolate, cookies and other high-fat foods for treating a low, because fat slows absorption.
why: Fat and protein delay stomach emptying, so a chocolate bar takes much longer to fix a low and then pushes glucose up for hours afterwards.
sources: Diabetes Canada CPG Ch. 14 Hypoglycemia, 2018, https://www.diabetes.ca/for-professionals/full-guidelines/chapter-14
Diabetes Canada patient resource: Lows and highs, https://www.diabetes.ca/managing-my-diabetes/tools---resources/lows-and-highs-blood-sugar-levels

title: Ask about a flatter long-acting insulin (Tresiba or Toujeo)
advice: If overnight lows keep happening despite tweaks, ask your doctor whether Tresiba (degludec) or Toujeo might suit you. Many people say their nights got calmer.
how: In Canada both are generally covered on many plans. People switching report needing a few days to a week to see the real effect, and that it is not always a 1:1 dose swap.
why: These insulins release more evenly over 24+ hours, with less of a peak; the SWITCH 1 trial found fewer nighttime lows with degludec vs glargine in type 1.
caveat: Tresiba's long tail means changes take 3-4 days to show; Toujeo can take several days too. Switching needs a prescriber.
sources: AJMC, 'Advera finds fewer overnight events with Tresiba' (SWITCH 1 summary), https://www.ajmc.com/view/advera-finds-fewer-overnight-events-with-tresiba
Diabetes UK Forum, 'Changing from Lantus to Tresiba - advice please', https://forum.diabetes.org.uk/boards/threads/changing-from-lantus-to-tresiba-advice-please.62814

title: Bringing down the swings (CV)
advice: Your swings are larger than the target. The good news is that most of the improvement comes from avoiding lows and the rebounds that follow them, and from steadier meal timing. Not from extra insulin.
how: Target CV is 36% or less. Main levers: fewer lows (each one tends to cause a rebound), measured treatment of lows, no stacked corrections, pre-bolusing when in range, consistent injection sites (avoid lumpy spots), and regular meal timing. Above 36%, the consensus regards hypoglycemia risk as substantially higher.
why: High CV goes along with more frequent lows, and lows followed by rebounds push the CV up further.
sources: Battelino T et al., International Consensus on Time in Range, Diabetes Care 2019, https://doi.org/10.2337/dci19-0028
Danne T et al., Diabetes Care 2017, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc17-1600

title: Wait out the CGM lag before eating more
advice: The hardest part of treating a low is waiting. Your sensor runs behind your blood, so it'll still look low for a while after the sugar is already working.
how: Treat, set a 15-minute phone timer, and do something else (sit down, sip water). Only re-treat if the G7 arrow is still flat or down after 15-20 min. Many people say 'trust the timer, not the panic'.
why: CGM reads interstitial fluid, which lags blood glucose by about 5-15 minutes, more when levels are changing fast.
caveat: If you feel worse or are under 3.0 at 15 min, re-treat right away.
sources: diaTribe, 'Defeating the Hypoglycemia Binge', https://diatribe.org/diabetes-management/defeating-hypoglycemia-binge
Diabetes UK Forum, 'Bad BG readings' (half-correction advice), https://forum.diabetes.org.uk/boards/threads/bad-bg-readings.87199/latest
Breakthrough T1D Forum, '15/15 rule outdated? If so, what is better way?', https://forum.breakthrought1d.org/t/15-15-rule-outdated-if-so-what-is-better-way/75173

title: A short walk after eating
advice: A 10-15 minute easy walk after a meal is one of the most reliable ways to blunt a spike, and it works in type 1 too. It's especially handy after a big or carb-heavy meal.
how: Start walking within about 15-30 minutes of finishing. Keep it gentle. Bring a fast carb along, because walking soon after a full rapid-insulin dose can push you low - if lows follow walks, that's a dose question for your team.
why: Working muscles take up glucose without needing extra insulin, lowering the post-meal peak.
sources: Manohar C et al. The effect of walking on postprandial glycemic excursion in patients with type 1 diabetes and healthy people. Diabetes Care, 2012, https://doi.org/10.2337/dc11-2381

title: Look at the arrow, not just the number
advice: A 5.5 heading straight down is a very different situation from a 5.5 sitting flat. The arrow tells you what's coming.
how: Act early on arrows: 6.0 with a down-arrow before driving or bed means a few grams now; 9.0 with a flat arrow 2 hours after a meal may need nothing.
why: Sugar Surfing's main point: direction and speed matter as much as the reading.
sources: Dr. Stephen Ponder, Sugar Surfing presentation slides, https://abcd10.redhot.circle-interactive.co.uk/sites/default/files/resources/IPN17%20PONDER.pdf

title: Foods that are slow for treating lows
advice: Chocolate, cookies, ice cream and peanut butter feel comforting during a low, but the fat slows the sugar down - so you stay low longer and often eat more. Many people then rebound high later.
how: Treat first with pure fast sugar (tablets, juice, regular pop), then have the slower foods afterward if your next meal is far off. Keep fast options where lows happen so you're not stuck with what's in the cupboard.
why: Fat delays stomach emptying, so carbs in chocolate or peanut butter reach the blood much more slowly than glucose.
